lessons.title: Adversarial generation: train two competing models
lessons.description: Watch a generator learn a two-mode distribution and diagnose mode collapse.
lessons.html:
Adversarial generation: train two competing models

Tag: Runnable implementation lab. Scope: an inspectable teaching implementation with real fitting, evaluation, and generated artifacts. This is not a production deployment certification.

Learning outcome: Watch a generator learn a two-mode distribution and diagnose mode collapse.

Where this appears in the real world

Adversarial training has been used for image synthesis and image-to-image translation. The simplest way to understand its dynamics is a one-dimensional target distribution, where missing modes are obvious. This lab learns numbers around -2 and +2 rather than generating full images.

Build the mental model

A generator maps random noise into samples. A discriminator learns to distinguish training-like samples from generated samples. The generator is updated to make its outputs harder for the discriminator to reject. The two objectives interact, so neither loss is a complete quality score.

Work through a concrete example

The target has roughly half its samples near -2 and half near +2. A generator that produces only values near +2 can look locally plausible while completely missing half the target. This is mode collapse, and a histogram makes it easier to see.

Follow the algorithm

  1. Draw independent samples from the synthetic two-mode target.
  2. Update the discriminator using real samples and detached generated samples.
  3. Freeze discriminator parameters while updating the generator through its scores.
  4. Alternate these updates for a bounded number of steps.
  5. Draw fresh target and generated samples and compare their distributions.
flowchart TD
 A[Random noise] --> B[Generator]
 B --> C[Generated samples]
 D[Real samples] --> E[Discriminator]
 C --> E
 E --> F[Discriminator update]
 E --> G[Generator update through scores]
 G --> B
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Random noise] --> B[Generator]
 B --> C[Generated samples]
 D[Real samples] --> E[Discriminator]
 C --> E
 E --> F[Discriminator update]
 E --> G[Generator update through scores]
 G --> B

Go one level deeper

The discriminator uses binary cross-entropy with logits. Detaching generated samples during its update prevents that loss from changing the generator. Freezing discriminator parameters during the generator update still permits gradients through the discriminator’s computation into the generator. Training can oscillate, collapse, or fail to converge. The saved generator is a tiny demonstration, not an image model.

Run the implementation

Use this lesson’s Practice buttons. For interpreter setup, external Windows commands, and fresh output folders, read the shared experiment workflow.

text
python foundations.py adversarial --steps 200 --output outputs/adversarial-short-{run}
text
python foundations.py adversarial --steps 1200 --output outputs/adversarial-long-{run}

Inspect the evidence

Open distribution.png. Compare both modes, spread, and fraction_generated_below_zero. A value near one-half does not by itself prove a correct distribution; inspect shape and standard deviation too.

Change one thing and prove what happened

Run the longer experiment with a second seed after documenting the first. Explain whether more training improved coverage or caused collapse. Submit a failure analysis even if the generated distribution remains poor.

Debugging checkpoint

Never mark the lab successful merely because generator loss decreases. A discriminator can become weak, saturated, or uninformative while sample quality remains poor.

Compute plan

The bundled exercise runs on a local central processing unit. For a larger version, measure runtime and memory before considering the optional graphics-processor path.

Build from start to finish: Synthetic scalar generator for simulator experiments

  1. Decision and data contract. Samples from a known two-mode distribution provide a controlled target. Replacing it with business data requires permission, coverage checks, and privacy evaluation. Define the acceptable error or failure rate before selecting a model.
  2. Architecture and training. Alternate discriminator and generator updates for a one-dimensional two-mode target. The Practice commands and algorithm above are the runnable implementation for this prototype.
  3. Independent evidence and comparison. Compare fresh target and generated draws after each training budget. There is no train/validation/test partition; --split does not apply. This simulator comparison is not a production final test.
  4. Save, reload, and use a new input. Retain the generated manifest, learned state, and input example. Use Load saved example and Predict new input. Two noise values produce one synthetic scalar. The model is deliberately one-dimensional and is not an image generator.
  5. Local deployment and production gap. The local saved-input interface is the serving prototype. Before external use, validate representative inputs, enforce request/access limits, and keep a versioned rollback artifact. The teaching score alone is not a deployment approval.
  6. Monitor. Mode coverage, sample distribution, seed sensitivity, and collapse despite plausible training losses. Name a response owner and a condition that would trigger review or rollback.

Evidence for this build

lessons.title: Statistical language models: count before you train a network
lessons.description: Build an inspectable word predictor with counts, smoothing, and perplexity.
lessons.html:
Statistical language models: count before you train a network

Tag: Runnable implementation lab. Scope: an inspectable teaching implementation with real fitting, evaluation, and generated artifacts. This is not a production deployment certification.

Learning outcome: Build an inspectable word predictor with counts, smoothing, and perplexity.

Where this appears in the real world

Short-context statistical language models provide useful baselines and make next-token prediction concrete. They help engineers distinguish the definition of a language model from the particular neural architecture used by modern assistants.

Build the mental model

Count how often a word follows a short context in training text. Convert those counts into a probability distribution. At prediction time, use the most recent context words to score or sample the next word. No neural-network parameters are required.

Work through a concrete example

If “server” is followed by “starts” three times and “stops” once, the unsmoothed probabilities are 0.75 and 0.25. Add-one smoothing adds one count to every vocabulary option before normalization, reserving probability for events not observed in training.

Follow the algorithm

  1. Create distinct short operations sentences and split them.
  2. Build vocabulary and context counts using only training sentences.
  3. Apply add-one smoothing to each context distribution.
  4. Score held-out tokens using their available context.
  5. Compute perplexity and sample a continuation from the learned distribution.
flowchart TD
 A[Training sentences] --> B[Vocabulary and counts]
 B --> C[Smoothed distributions]
 D[Recent context words] --> E[Select context distribution]
 C --> E
 E --> F[Score next word]
 E --> G[Sample next word]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Training sentences] --> B[Vocabulary and counts]
 B --> C[Smoothed distributions]
 D[Recent context words] --> E[Select context distribution]
 C --> E
 E --> F[Score next word]
 E --> G[Sample next word]

Go one level deeper

An order-two model uses one previous word; an order-three model uses two. Start and end markers define sentence boundaries. Unknown evaluation words map to an explicit unknown symbol. Perplexity is the exponential of average negative log probability, using natural logarithms here. Lower perplexity indicates better probability assignment only under compatible tokenization, vocabulary handling, and evaluation data.

Run the implementation

Use this lesson’s Practice buttons. For interpreter setup, external Windows commands, and fresh output folders, read the shared experiment workflow.

text
python foundations.py ngram --order 1 --output outputs/ngram-one-{run}
text
python foundations.py ngram --order 3 --output outputs/ngram-three-{run}

Inspect the evidence

Inspect token-probabilities.png and compare perplexity with uniform_baseline_perplexity. The generated text is sampled from actual counts; it may be awkward because the corpus is small and smoothing spreads probability widely.

Change one thing and prove what happened

Hand-calculate one context’s smoothed probability from counts. Compare order one with order three and explain why longer context can create data sparsity instead of automatically improving results.

Debugging checkpoint

Do not compare this word-level perplexity directly with the byte-level perplexity of the scratch neural language model. The prediction units differ.

Compute plan

The bundled exercise runs on a local central processing unit. This scikit-learn or small-table implementation does not gain automatic graphics-processor acceleration.

  1. Decision and data contract. Training sentences tokenized into words; vocabulary and context counts are learned from the training split. Real logs require removal of secrets and stable tokenization. Define the acceptable error or failure rate before selecting a model.
  2. Architecture and training. Count training contexts, construct the vocabulary, and apply add-one smoothing. The Practice commands and algorithm above are the runnable implementation for this prototype.
  3. Independent evidence and comparison. Compare orders 1 and 3 on identical held-out sentences and the included uniform-vocabulary perplexity baseline.
  4. Save, reload, and use a new input. Retain the generated manifest, learned state, and input example. Use Load saved example and Predict new input. A distribution over the next word for a supplied context. The saved counting model needs no neural framework.
  5. Local deployment and production gap. The local saved-input interface is the serving prototype. Before external use, validate representative inputs, enforce request/access limits, and keep a versioned rollback artifact. The teaching score alone is not a deployment approval.
  6. Monitor. Held-out perplexity, unknown-word rate, memory growth with context order, and inappropriate memorized text. Name a response owner and a condition that would trigger review or rollback.

Evidence for this build

A normalized next-word distribution, unknown-word behavior, comparable perplexities, and new-context predictions. Include the measured reports and one limitation. lessons.title: Reinforcement learning: learn actions from rewards
lessons.description: Train a complete small action-value learner and compare it with random behavior.
lessons.html:
Reinforcement learning: learn actions from rewards

Tag: Runnable implementation lab. Scope: an inspectable teaching implementation with real fitting, evaluation, and generated artifacts. This is not a production deployment certification.

Learning outcome: Train a complete small action-value learner and compare it with random behavior.

Where this appears in the real world

Routing, scheduling, and simulated robot control involve actions whose consequences unfold over time. Reinforcement learning studies how a policy can improve from interaction. Our four-by-four grid is an explicit educational environment, not an autonomous real-world control system.

Build the mental model

The agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward, and sees a new state. A table estimates the value of each action in each state. Updates combine immediate reward with an estimate of future reward. Exploration allows the agent to discover actions it has not yet learned to prefer.

Work through a concrete example

If an action currently has value 2, its target is 6, and the learning rate is 0.2, the updated value is 2 + 0.2 × (6 - 2) = 2.8. At the terminal goal, the target uses the immediate reward without adding a future-state value.

Follow the algorithm

  1. Initialize a table for sixteen states and four possible actions.
  2. Choose random actions some of the time and otherwise choose the current best action.
  3. Move in the grid, receive a step penalty or goal reward, and update the chosen entry.
  4. Reduce exploration over training episodes.
  5. Evaluate the greedy policy without exploration and compare with random actions.
flowchart TD
 A[Observe state] --> B{Explore?}
 B -->|Yes| C[Random action]
 B -->|No| D[Best table action]
 C --> E[Environment transition]
 D --> E
 E --> F[Reward and next state]
 F --> G[Update action value]
 G --> A
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Observe state] --> B{Explore?}
 B -->|Yes| C[Random action]
 B -->|No| D[Best table action]
 C --> E[Environment transition]
 D --> E
 E --> F[Reward and next state]
 F --> G[Update action value]
 G --> A

Go one level deeper

The update is tabular Q-learning; Q denotes an action-value function, not an acronym. The discount factor controls how future rewards contribute. The goal is a terminal state; the 50-step cap truncates an unfinished trajectory. The terminal goal removes the future-value term, whereas this time-limit truncation is not a new terminal goal. The environment is deterministic and all evaluation episodes begin at the same state, so repeated success does not establish generalization to new maps. A neural value function is an extension, not a requirement for reinforcement learning.

Run the implementation

Use this lesson’s Practice buttons. For interpreter setup, external Windows commands, and fresh output folders, read the shared experiment workflow.

text
python foundations.py reinforcement --episodes 50 --output outputs/reinforcement-short-{run}
text
python foundations.py reinforcement --episodes 500 --output outputs/reinforcement-long-{run}

Inspect the evidence

Open rewards.png. Training rewards include exploration, while greedy_success_rate is measured without it. Interpret greedy_policy using the report’s action_order. Compare greedy_mean_return with random_mean_return.

Change one thing and prove what happened

Trace a greedy path from the upper-left corner to the lower-right goal. Explain the terminal-state update. In a copied environment introduce an obstacle and evaluate the old policy before retraining, documenting what fails.

Debugging checkpoint

Reward design can encourage unintended behavior. A large reward score is only useful when the environment and reward represent the desired task faithfully.

Compute plan

The bundled exercise runs on a local central processing unit. This scikit-learn or small-table implementation does not gain automatic graphics-processor acceleration.

Build from start to finish: Sequential route decisions in a small simulator

  1. Decision and data contract. States, permitted actions, transition rules, rewards, termination, and episode length define the data-generating environment. Define the acceptable error or failure rate before selecting a model.
  2. Architecture and training. Train a tabular action-value policy through rewards in the deterministic 4-by-4 grid. The Practice commands and algorithm above are the runnable implementation for this prototype.
  3. Independent evidence and comparison. Compare greedy and random policies over 100 episodes each in the same map and start state. --split does not apply; a new-map evaluation is a separate extension.
  4. Save, reload, and use a new input. Retain the generated manifest, learned state, and input example. Use Load saved example and Predict new input. An action index for an integer state: zero up, one right, two down, three left. Physical deployment is outside this lab.
  5. Local deployment and production gap. The local saved-input interface is the serving prototype. Before external use, validate representative inputs, enforce request/access limits, and keep a versioned rollback artifact. The teaching score alone is not a deployment approval.
  6. Monitor. Success rate, episode return, unsafe actions, reward exploitation, and transfer failure on changed maps. Name a response owner and a condition that would trigger review or rollback.

Evidence for this build

A terminal-aware value update, reward curve, greedy/random returns, a saved-table decision, and limits of same-map success. Include the measured reports and one limitation. lessons.html:
Lab 22 Run inference and inspect tokens

Concept: inference is using fixed learned parameters to produce an output. A tokenizer turns text into integer identifiers. The model maps identifiers to vectors, processes context and predicts scores for the next token. A decoding rule chooses a token, then repeats.

The bundle includes a model revision lock. The following command preserves the existing pin. If you begin without a lock, it resolves the model repository's current commit and records it. Do not refresh it in the middle of an experiment.

bash
python lab.py lock
python lab.py tokenize --prompt "A model predicts the next token."
python lab.py infer --prompt "Explain a neural network in one sentence."

First use downloads the tokenizer, model configuration and weight file. Later runs reuse the cache. Inference runs on your computer; this code does not send your prompt to a hosted generation application programming interface. The download itself still requires network access.

Expected: token identifiers, token pieces, a reconstructed sentence, a chat template and a generated answer. Exact answers may differ across environments. The model can be wrong or repetitive. Seeing output proves the pipeline works; it does not prove answer quality.

The script calls apply_chat_template because the checkpoint expects conversation roles in a particular format. The assistant response is still a continuation of a token sequence. add_generation_prompt=True marks where the assistant's reply begins. [2]

Read the code: in lab.py, find load, messages and generate. Explain these operations:

  1. from_pretrained loads existing learned weights.
  2. .eval() changes behaviors such as dropout; it does not disable gradients by itself.
  3. torch.inference_mode() avoids gradient tracking during generation.
  4. max_new_tokens bounds generated output, not input prompt length.
  5. The output is sliced after the input-token count, so the prompt is not printed as part of the answer.

Experiment: run the same prompt with --temperature 0, then --temperature 0.8. Repeat the latter with --seed 43 and --seed 44. The default seed is fixed; a repeated run with the same seed can repeat its sampled output. Temperature rescales scores before sampling. It changes the selection distribution, not the stored knowledge.

Checkpoint: explain the difference between a token and a word, between weights and activations, and between model loading time and generation time.

Extension: try punctuation, a Python function and a non-English sentence in the tokenizer. Observe token counts rather than assuming a fixed number of characters per token.

lessons.title: See the numbers underneath
lessons.description: Connect tensors, probabilities, loss and gradients.
lessons.html:
Lab 23 Understand the mathematics one piece at a time

Start with four objects:

ObjectBeginner meaningTechnical meaning
ScalarOne numberA rank-zero tensor
VectorA list of numbersA rank-one tensor
MatrixA grid of numbersA rank-two tensor
TensorA general arrayAn array with any number of axes

For a batch of two sequences of 16 tokens, token identifiers have shape [2, 16]. After a 576-dimensional embedding lookup, the representation has shape [2, 16, 576]. The chosen checkpoint's hidden width is 576; inspect its configuration instead of assuming every small language model uses that width.

A linear layer computes y = xW + b under one common matrix convention. Its weights are learned numbers. An activation function adds nonlinearity. Attention lets a token use information from permitted earlier positions. A feed-forward network transforms its representation. The output head produces one score per vocabulary entry. Those raw scores are called logits.

Softmax converts logits into probabilities. If the correct next token receives probability 0.1, its negative log-likelihood is -ln(0.1) ≈ 2.303. At probability 0.8, the loss is approximately 0.223. Lower loss means the model assigns more probability to the correct tokens on that dataset.

A gradient tells us how a small parameter change would affect loss. Gradient descent subtracts a scaled gradient: new_weight = old_weight - learning_rate × gradient. Backpropagation computes gradients efficiently through the computation. The optimizer decides how to turn them into parameter updates.

Hands-on: run python mechanisms.py --demo math. Inspect softmax probabilities and negative log-likelihood. In the one-weight example, prediction is weight × 2 and target is 6. At weight 1, squared error is 16 and its gradient is −16. A step of size 0.1 changes the weight to 2.6, prediction to 5.2, and squared error to 0.64. Explain why subtracting the negative gradient increases the weight.

Checkpoint: if training loss improves while validation loss worsens, can you explain why the model may be memorizing its training examples?

More technical: next-token training usually uses logits at positions 0...T-2 to predict labels at 1...T-1. Hugging Face causal-language model classes shift labels internally. Our scratch model constructs shifted targets explicitly. Doing both shifts would train the wrong task.

Attention without unexplained shorthand

Attention combines information using learned scores. Imagine the current position needs to resolve a relationship in the preceding text. Each position's representation is transformed into three different kinds of vectors:

  • Query vectors: representations used to score what information the current position should use.
  • Key vectors: representations against which queries are compared.
  • Value vectors: the information combined using the resulting attention weights.

The familiar letters Q, K and V are mathematical symbols for query, key and value matrices. They are not names of three separate databases.

In a common attention calculation, queries are multiplied by transposed keys, the scores are scaled, prohibited positions are masked, and softmax produces weights. A weighted sum of value vectors forms the result. Multiple attention heads perform versions of this operation in parallel representation subspaces.

If three permitted positions receive illustrative weights 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1, the attention result is 0.6 × value_1 + 0.3 × value_2 + 0.1 × value_3. Those are vectors, so the multiplication and addition apply across their components.

A key–value cache stores previously computed key and value representations during supported autoregressive inference. It avoids repeating some earlier computation, but storing more context usually costs more cache memory. The cache is temporary runtime state, not a second set of trained model weights.

Check yourself: why can a longer conversation use more memory even though the model's parameter count has not changed? More context can require more cached representations, activations and temporary work.

lessons.html:
Lab 24 Build an honest baseline

Project: classify an machine learning support ticket into environment, memory or data, returning exactly {"label":"memory"} or the corresponding other label. This is intentionally narrow so that evaluation is understandable.

The supplied original synthetic dataset has 36 training examples, 12 validation examples and 12 final test examples. Each split is balanced. Exact texts are disjoint. Similar concepts occur across splits, so this is a classroom benchmark, not evidence of broad real-world performance.

bash
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python lab.py eval --split validation --output outputs/baseline-validation.json

The generated report in JavaScript Object Notation contains every output, the expected label, the parsed prediction, strict schema validity, accuracy and timing. The parser rejects extra prose, extra keys and invalid categories. A semantically plausible answer in the wrong format is a failure for this contract.

Three different questions:

  1. Is the answer valid JavaScript Object Notation with exactly the permitted schema?
  2. Does the selected label match the expected label?
  3. Does it arrive within the application's latency and memory budget?

For a memory-exhaustion ticket, {"label":"memory"} can satisfy both format and category checks. It looks like memory. fails the format contract; {"label":"data"} can pass the schema while choosing the wrong category.

Inspect failures in order: input parsing, task/annotation ambiguity, predicted content, output parsing, then the loaded model and adapter. This baseline does not retrieve notes. Record output length with latency: a shorter answer can arrive sooner even when its token rate is lower.

The supplied historical adapted-model run scored 11/12 on the final test, with valid structure on all 12. This is an archived classroom result, not your baseline or a promised outcome. Measure your own run and retain its failures.

Evaluation refuses to overwrite an existing report. On a rerun, choose a fresh filename and use that filename in the comparison command. Preserve the earlier evidence.

Why splits matter: training examples update weights; validation guides your design choices; the final test estimates performance after those choices are fixed. Repeatedly examining test failures and adjusting the model turns the test set into another validation set. Create a fresh independent test set if that happens.

Checkpoint: explain why a model with perfect training accuracy can still be useless on new tickets. Then identify one limitation of the supplied 12-example test: one example changes accuracy by about 8.3 percentage points.

Extension: create a simple keyword classifier as a non-neural baseline. It may be sufficient for a narrow task. Comparing it to a small language model is part of good engineering, not a failure to use advanced technology.

lessons.title: Teach with a small adapter
lessons.description: Train low-rank updates and compare real outputs.
lessons.html:
Lab 25 Fine tune with low-rank adaptation and compare results

Concept: supervised fine-tuning teaches a model desired responses to examples. Full fine-tuning updates all chosen parameters. low-rank adaptation freezes the original weights and adds small trainable matrices to selected layers.

For a weight matrix, a common formulation is W_new = W_frozen + (alpha/r) × BA. The adapter rank r limits the size of the update. Here rank is 8, alpha is 16, and adapters attach to attention query and value projections. Query vectors participate in deciding which context is relevant; value vectors carry the information attention combines. [9]

Start with a five-update smoke test:

bash
python lab.py train --steps 5 --output outputs/smoke-adapter

Expected: a trainable-parameter count, finite losses and an adapter directory. A smoke test verifies that data encoding, forward pass, backward pass, optimizer update and saving work. It is not a quality experiment.

Then train a fresh experiment from the same original base:

bash
python lab.py train --steps 60 --output outputs/adapter-60
python lab.py eval --adapter outputs/adapter-60 --split validation --output outputs/adapter-validation.json
python compare_reports.py outputs/baseline-validation.json outputs/adapter-validation.json

The implementation refuses to overwrite a nonempty training output directory. Each run starts from the same base weights. The saved adapter must be loaded with the same base model and revision; it is not a standalone full model.

Read the code: encode_example builds a complete training conversation, masks prompt positions with -100, and supervises the assistant answer. The prompt still affects the answer through context. Masking it out of the loss does not remove it from the input.

collate pads sequences to a common batch length. Padding positions get attention mask 0 and label -100. Real end-of-sequence tokens remain supervised, even if the padding identifier equals the end-of-sequence identifier. Masking every occurrence of that shared identifier would be an error.

The model's causal loss shifts labels internally. loss.backward() computes gradients. Gradient clipping limits their overall norm. optimizer.step() updates trainable adapter parameters. zero_grad() clears gradients before the next update; otherwise gradients accumulate.

Memory drill: in a simple fully 32-bit floating-point adaptive moment estimation training setup, weights, gradients and two optimizer moment buffers alone cost approximately 16 bytes per trained parameter. For 135 million parameters that is about 2.16 gigabytes before activations and other overhead. Low-rank adaptation makes the trainable subset much smaller, but the frozen base and the activations needed for backpropagation still occupy memory. Batch size and sequence length therefore still matter.

Interpretation: compare validation accuracy and schema validity with the baseline, and look at the raw answers. Training loss improvement alone is insufficient. The before/after validation loss is answer-token negative log-likelihood, not a general language benchmark. The 60 updates sample training examples with replacement; they are not 60 epochs.

If validation is weak, change only one variable in the next run. Examples: reduce --lr from 0.001 to 0.0003, increase --steps, or improve representative training examples. Name each output differently. Do not repeatedly tune on the final test.

After choosing a setting using validation, evaluate both the base and chosen adapter on the final test:

bash
python lab.py eval --split test --output outputs/base-test.json
python lab.py eval --adapter outputs/adapter-60 --split test --output outputs/adapter-test.json

Checkpoint: explain what changed on disk, which parameters trained, why the base model remains necessary and what would count as evidence that tuning actually helped.

Extension: run seeds 42, 43 and 44, using separate output directories, to observe variance. For a stronger assessment, collect hundreds of reviewed examples, keep source documents or customer threads within one split, include ambiguous/out-of-scope cases and document annotation disagreements.

Build from start to finish: Adapt a compact assistant to structured support triage

Define allowed support categories and an output schema; curate independently labeled examples; freeze the base checkpoint; train low-rank adapter matrices; measure category accuracy and valid structure on validation; select settings; evaluate once on final test; save the adapter with the base revision and prompt contract; use the adapter in inference.

This exercise’s flow: Labeled ticket and chat template → frozen base plus trainable adapter → validation schema/category checks → selected adapter → final-test comparison.

Evidence for this lesson: Base revision, adapter path, trainable parameters, validation report pair, one schema/category failure, and a new-ticket response with the adapter. Keep the matching base and tokenizer.

lessons.title: Give the model useful notes
lessons.description: See retrieval and generation as separate steps.
lessons.html:
Lab 26 Add knowledge using retrieval

Concept: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant information and includes it in the prompt. It changes the model's current evidence without changing its weights. Fine-tuning can teach a format or behavior; retrieval-augmented generation is often better suited to facts that change frequently.

bash
python lab.py rag --prompt "How do I fix CUDA out of memory?" --retrieve-only
python lab.py rag --prompt "How do I fix CUDA out of memory?"

The supplied knowledge base has four short notes. Retrieval uses a transparent word-overlap score. It is intentionally not an embedding model, vector database or Best Matching 25 implementation. The first command shows retrieved notes; the second asks the model to answer from them.

Expected: a retrieval trace followed by an answer. Inspect whether the answer is actually supported and whether its citation points to the correct note. The small generator may still invent information. A grounding prompt and a citation-looking string do not guarantee factual grounding.

In our verification run, retrieval selected the appropriate memory note, but the answer repeated advice and omitted its citation. This is a concrete example of successful retrieval with weak generation. Treat fixing and evaluating that behavior as part of the exercise.

Test an unsupported question and a synonym-heavy question. The retriever's no-match branch provides an explicit no-evidence response, but lexical overlap can also retrieve an irrelevant note. Do not treat any match as proof of answerability.

Measure separately: retrieval hit rate asks whether the needed source was retrieved; answer correctness asks whether the generated answer is right; citation validity asks whether the cited source supports the claim.

Checkpoint: add a new factual note, rerun retrieval and explain why the model weights did not change.

Extension: replace overlap retrieval with a text-embedding model and cosine similarity. Store source identifiers, chunk boundaries and document versions. Build 20 question-to-source expectations before adjusting the chunking strategy. Compare retrieval quality before changing the generator.

  • Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering — Karpukhin et al. (2020) — Compare learned dense retrieval with this lesson's token-overlap retrieval; dense retrieval is an extension, not the implemented algorithm.

lessons.title: Train from random weights
lessons.description: Build a tiny byte-level language model from the beginning.
lessons.html:
Lab 27 Build a small language model from random weights

Concept: loading a pretrained model starts with useful learned parameters. Creating a model object from an architecture initializes new parameters; training must teach it patterns from the beginning.

bash
python scratch_lm.py --steps 300 --output outputs/my-first-pretrained-model

This exercise uses a roughly 137,000-parameter byte-level Transformer, much smaller than our working small language model range. It is a microscope for understanding training. Each Unicode Transformation Format with eight-bit code units byte is a token from a vocabulary of 256. The training corpus consists of generated educational sentences with random note numbers; validation uses a separately generated corpus from the same simple grammar.

The architecture has token embeddings, learned position embeddings, two Transformer blocks, layer normalization and a vocabulary output head. A causal mask blocks future-token information. The test suite checks that changing future input tokens cannot change earlier-position outputs.

Expected: finite training loss, validation loss measured before and after training; improvement is not guaranteed, generated fragments, a state dictionary and a report in JavaScript Object Notation. Early samples can be nonsense even while loss improves. This is especially visible after only 100 updates. Do not report this as a useful general-language model.

Read: batch builds shifted input/target pairs. ce flattens positions for cross-entropy. The script samples training windows, backpropagates, updates parameters and finally generates tokens one at a time.

Checkpoint: explain why the pretrained model with 135 million parameters is useful immediately while the scratch model begins with essentially random predictions. Then explain why a model could reduce loss on this repetitive synthetic grammar without learning general English.

Extension: write an original corpus of several thousand sentences and split by source passage. Increase context length, width or layers one at a time. Record parameter counts and runtime. Do not compare perplexity across unrelated tokenizers as if they used the same units; this script reports byte-token perplexity.

To reload your own checkpoint safely, instantiate the same architecture and load its state dictionary with torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True). Keep the architecture, vocabulary and context configuration with the weights.

Build from start to finish: Train a tiny operations-text language model

Run the bundled synthetic corpus with independently generated training and validation text. For a later real-corpus extension, define permitted operations documents and split whole documents before extracting sequences; build byte embeddings, causal attention, feed-forward layers, and an output head; train next-byte prediction; compare held-out loss; inspect generated text; save weights and vocabulary; package the tokenizer with inference.

This exercise’s flow: Synthetic text → byte IDs and shifted targets → causal model → held-out byte loss → checkpoint and configuration → sampled continuation.

Evidence for this lesson: Parameter count, before/after loss in byte-token units, causal-mask check, saved configuration, reload sample, and one incoherent completion.

lessons.title: Make the numbers smaller
lessons.description: Measure storage and reconstruction error.
lessons.html:
Lab 28 Understand quantization and memory

bash
python mechanisms.py --demo quantization

The quantization experiment creates a floating-point weight matrix, chooses a scale, rounds it to signed eight-bit values and reconstructs approximate floating-point weights. It prints stored bytes and mean squared reconstruction error.

The simplified equation is q = round(w / scale) and w_approx = q × scale. Rounding saves representation space and introduces error. Real schemes may use groups, different scales, zero points, nonlinear codebooks or mixed precision.

Hands-on modifications: run python mechanisms.py --demo quantization --qmax 7 to simulate a signed four-bit numerical range. This changes both the scale divisor and the clamp limit from 127 to 7; changing only the clamp would saturate many values. However, storing those values in an int8 tensor still consumes eight bits per element: packing two values into one byte is a separate engineering step. Report both numeric precision and actual storage size.

Checkpoint: explain why halving weight bytes does not necessarily halve total process random-access memory, and why a quantized model may be slower on hardware without an appropriate kernel.

Deployment extension: use a supported inference runtime such as llama.cpp and a checkpoint in the compatible .gguf format. Follow its current conversion and quantization instructions for the chosen model; record the runtime commit, quantization type and original model revision. Reuse your saved evaluation prompts and compare accuracy, resident memory, warm latency and tokens per second. [11]

Quantized low-rank adaptation extension: on a supported graphics processing unit setup, load a base using a bitsandbytes quantization configuration, prepare it for k-bit training, then attach adapters. This is a separate exercise; the provided low-rank adaptation trainer deliberately uses 32-bit floating-point precision to avoid mixing hardware-specific quantization debugging into the first training lab. Review the current compatibility documentation before changing its loader. [10]

Build from start to finish: Prepare a compact model for an edge memory budget

Measure the full runtime memory first; choose precision and supported runtime; quantify rounding error on the numerical lab; for an actual compressed checkpoint, compare task quality, memory, and latency against the uncompressed baseline; preserve tokenizer and serving settings. The supplied code is a numerical compression demonstration, not a production checkpoint converter.

This exercise’s flow: Floating-point matrix → scale and integer rounding → reconstructed matrix → error and actual storage comparison.

Evidence for this lesson: Integer range, scale, reconstruction mean squared error, and actual tensor bytes including the scale. Explain why an int8 tensor using a four-bit numerical range is not packed four-bit storage. No model is trained or saved.

lessons.title: Learn from a teacher
lessons.description: Understand teacher signals, student learning and pruning.
lessons.html:
Lab 29 Distillation and pruning

The distillation demonstration in mechanisms.py gives a student logits tensor a gradient toward a teacher probability distribution. Temperature softens the distributions. The example uses Kullback–Leibler divergence and multiplies by temperature squared, a conventional compensation for gradient scaling.

Checkpoint: explain how learning from a probability distribution conveys more information than only learning the teacher's single most likely class.

Practical distillation project:

  1. Define a narrow task and create a validation/test set independently of teacher generation.
  2. Select a larger teacher whose outputs you are permitted to use. Run a small quality sample before generating a large dataset.
  3. Give the teacher new training prompts and store its answers plus provenance. Do not include final test prompts.
  4. Validate formats and manually review a sample. Remove incorrect or ambiguous answers instead of treating the teacher as ground truth.
  5. Train the student on the reviewed outputs using the same supervised-training pattern from Lab 25.
  6. Compare the student, untuned base, teacher and a simple baseline on the untouched test set. Include latency and cost.

This is sequence-level distillation: teacher text becomes training data. Token-distribution distillation needs compatible vocabularies or an explicit alignment method. Matching probability vector indices from unrelated tokenizers is invalid.

Pruning activity: zero the lowest-magnitude 20 percent of weights in a copy of the scratch model. Evaluate loss before and after, then time it. The tensor shapes are unchanged, so a normal dense kernel can do the same amount of work. To obtain practical speedups, investigate structured removal or kernels that exploit the exact sparse pattern. Do not assert a speed gain just because many entries are zero.

Assessment: explain the difference between reducing stored precision, reducing parameter structure and teaching a smaller student. Each has different failure modes and measurement requirements.

Build from start to finish: Design a small student for a narrow support task

Define the student task and independent test set; obtain permitted teacher outputs only for training examples; choose soft-target or response-based learning; train student parameters; compare with the student trained without teacher signals; save a versioned model; assess cost and failure cases. The included code computes soft teacher targets and a student-logit gradient. A complete student training loop, pruning, and production text distillation are separate implementation activities.

This exercise’s flow: Teacher/student logits → temperature-scaled distributions → divergence loss → student-logit gradient.

Evidence for this lesson: Teacher probabilities, student gradient signs, and a temperature comparison. Explain the update that could follow. The demonstration performs no optimizer step and produces no trained-student checkpoint; pruning must be implemented separately.

lessons.title: Evaluate a coding model
lessons.description: Use executable tests to judge generated programs.
lessons.html:
Lab 30 Specialize for code and structured outputs

bash
python lab.py lock --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct
python lab.py infer --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct --prompt "Write a Python function that returns the maximum of a nonempty list." --max-new-tokens 128

This model switch introduces a code-specialized checkpoint while keeping the inference interface familiar. It needs more memory than the model with 135 million parameters. The command is an extension, not a claim that this model is the best current coding model. [7]

Build an evaluation: write ten tiny function specifications and tests before collecting model outputs. Include empty-input behavior, negative values, duplicates and incorrect types where relevant. Manually extract and inspect generated functions, then run tests in a disposable environment with no credentials and no network. A timeout is necessary but is not a complete sandbox.

Measure the fraction of tasks whose first answer passes all tests. Keep sampling settings fixed. A function that looks plausible or explains itself fluently has not demonstrated correctness.

Fine-tuning activity: adapt the training row format from tickets to function specifications and approved reference implementations. Preserve assistant-only loss masking and separate tasks by family or repository to reduce leakage. Compare instruction tuning to a prompt-only baseline first.

For a later coding agent, separate proposal, execution and evaluation. The model proposes an edit; a restricted runner executes checks; a verifier records evidence. Model capability and permission to act are independent design decisions. Keep the first agent limited to a disposable exercise repository.

Checkpoint: explain why passing three examples is not proof that a generated program is correct, and why a benchmark must define its sampling and execution policy.

Build from start to finish: Build a local coding-assistant prototype

Choose a small pretrained coding checkpoint and permitted programming tasks; pin its revision; run generation; assess outputs using independent tests in a suitable isolated execution environment; track correctness and latency; package prompts, model revision, and test cases. This lesson runs a pretrained model; it does not train a coding foundation model from scratch.

This exercise’s flow: Function specification → coding checkpoint → generated source → inspect/extract code → independently authored tests in a disposable runner.

Evidence for this lesson: Task and test manifest, checkpoint and sampling settings, first-answer pass fraction, a failing input, and latency/output length. This is pretrained inference; no trained coding-model artifact is produced.

lessons.title: Connect images and language
lessons.description: Upload your own image and inspect the actual response.
lessons.html:
Lab 31 Add images

Use the image-upload form in this lesson’s Practice tab with a simple image you own, such as a photo of a mug. This exercise uses a pretrained vision-language model and an image processor. For an external terminal, place sample.jpg inside the lab/ folder, activate the lab environment and run the command below from that folder.

bash
python lab.py lock --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM-256M-Instruct
python vision_lab.py sample.jpg --prompt "What objects are visible?"

The model card is the reference for the checkpoint and interface. [8] The script uses the Transformers 4.57 teaching environment; a newer major release may expose a different auto-model class. If the optional vision dependency stack is incompatible, report the exact error rather than changing the already-working text environment in place.

Concept: the image processor resizes and normalizes pixels. The vision encoder turns image patches into features. A connecting component makes those features usable by the language component. The language decoder generates text conditioned on the image representation and prompt.

Assessment: test five images with questions whose answers you can verify. Include counts, colors and an image with no relevant object. Record confident mistakes. Small vision models are not reliable substitutes for specialized optical character recognition or exact measurement tools.

Build activity: for a controlled training experiment, create labeled images of simple shapes. Split by rendered scene rather than nearly identical image variants. Begin by freezing a pretrained vision encoder and language model, training only the connecting projection where the architecture supports it. Then compare to tuning additional modules. This requires an image-text dataset and a multimodal loss pipeline; the text-only ticket trainer is not a drop-in vision-language model trainer.

Checkpoint: explain which tensors come from text, which come from pixels and where the modalities interact. State what the task evaluates rather than claiming general visual understanding.

Build from start to finish: Build a screenshot-description prototype

Choose a small vision-language checkpoint; pin its revision; prepare permitted images and reference answers; feed pixels through the model processor; generate a description; compare factual details and unsupported claims; record latency and memory; define a rejection behavior for unclear images. This lesson implements pretrained inference, not vision-language pretraining.

This exercise’s flow: Image and question → multimodal processor → image-conditioned model → description → compare with visible facts.

lessons.title: Experiment with other families
lessons.description: Train tiny expert, state-space and hybrid models.
lessons.html:
Lab 32 Explore mixture of experts state space and hybrid models

Run the architecture demonstration first:

bash
python mechanisms.py --demo architectures

ToyMoE uses a learned router to select one of four feed-forward experts per token. It prints token counts per expert. All experts exist in memory even when only one executes for a token. The implementation omits production features such as capacity limits, expert parallelism and load-balancing losses.

Experiment: make one router bias much larger than the others. Observe expert collapse: most tokens go to one expert. Explain why training should monitor routing distribution, not only language-model loss.

ToySSM implements a diagonal linear state recurrence: state_t = decay × state_(t-1) + input_projection(x_t). It is a simple state space model illustration, not Mamba. The test suite verifies that processing a sequence in two chunks with carried state matches processing it as one sequence.

Train tiny end-to-end language models using these components:

bash
python scratch_lm.py --architecture ssm --steps 100 --output outputs/toy-ssm
python scratch_lm.py --architecture moe --steps 100 --output outputs/toy-moe
python scratch_lm.py --architecture hybrid --steps 100 --output outputs/toy-hybrid

The mixture of experts version retains causal attention and uses routed feed-forward blocks. The state space model version replaces the sequence-mixing component with recurrence. The hybrid uses a state space model mixer and an attention mixer. All use the same byte vocabulary and synthetic corpus generation. They are teaching prototypes with different parameter counts, not faithful reproductions of vendor models or a fair research benchmark.

Measure: parameters, loss, wall-clock time and memory. Then normalize model sizes or compute budgets before making an architectural comparison. Our state space model uses a Python loop and will not demonstrate optimized Mamba throughput. The scratch generator recomputes context windows; it is not a fast state-cached state space model serving implementation.

Professional extension: reproduce an official Mamba or hybrid-model example in a separate environment, using its documented graphics processing unit and kernel requirements. Compare at fixed prompt and output lengths, separate prefill from decoding, and test both quality and long-context recall. Do not infer unlimited memory or perfect recall from a fixed-size state. [5, 6]

Checkpoint: distinguish total parameters, parameters used per token, arithmetic work, memory bandwidth and actual measured latency.

Build from start to finish: Compare three sequence engines for streamed event text

Keep corpus, split, training steps, and evaluation fixed. Train the supplied toy mixture-of-experts, state-space, and hybrid alternatives. Inspect routing or state behavior, measured loss, saved checkpoints, and memory/runtime. A toy state-space model does not reproduce the full Mamba algorithm.

This exercise’s flow: Shared synthetic corpus → expert routing or recurrent-state updates → next-byte scores → comparable loss calculation → separate model checkpoints.

Evidence for this lesson: Total parameters and runtime per model, routing counts or chunked-state check, loss and samples. Explain why unequal model sizes and Python implementations prevent a hardware speed ranking.

lessons.title: Move an experiment to a graphics processor
lessons.description: Plan a rental, verify the device and preserve your work.
lessons.html:
Rent compute only when an experiment needs it

Concept — Cloud architecture, cost planning, and a documented deployment procedure. The commands are intended to run a real lab on a rental, but this release was verified locally; no paid Vast.ai instance was rented during verification.

The decision before spending money

All 18 foundation experiments use small datasets and run on a central processing unit. Complete them locally first. A graphics processing unit becomes useful when you scale neural-network training, enlarge image batches, or adapt a language model that exceeds your laptop's practical memory or runtime. Renting a graphics processor does not automatically accelerate scikit-learn's ordinary tree or regression implementations.

Measure a local baseline: model, number of examples, batch size, sequence length, memory use, and elapsed time. Decide what would make a rental worthwhile. For example, a larger visual-inspection experiment might require training thousands of high-resolution images. The included convolution lab uses small eight-by-eight images and does not justify a rental by itself.

Architecture and data flow

flowchart TD
 A[Windows browser] --> B[Local tunnel port 8766]
 B --> C[Encrypted Secure Shell connection]
 C --> D[Remote loopback port 8765]
 D --> E[Course Python server]
 E --> F[Neural training process]
 F --> G[Graphics processor]
 F --> H[Reports and checkpoints]
 H --> I[Download to Windows]
 H --> J[Optional attached volume]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Windows browser] --> B[Local tunnel port 8766]
 B --> C[Encrypted Secure Shell connection]
 C --> D[Remote loopback port 8765]
 D --> E[Course Python server]
 E --> F[Neural training process]
 F --> G[Graphics processor]
 F --> H[Reports and checkpoints]
 H --> I[Download to Windows]
 H --> J[Optional attached volume]

The website and training run on the rented machine. Your browser displays the interface through a private tunnel. The course server remains bound to the remote loopback address. A cloud rental is a real computer environment, not a browser simulation.

1. Choose a small, compatible rental

Create your Vast.ai account, enable the available account protections, and inspect the live marketplace. Choose a single graphics processor before considering multi-device training. A 24-gigabyte NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 or RTX 4090 is a possible starting configuration for larger experiments; it is not a promise that every model will fit. Weight precision, optimizer state, activations, batch size, and context length all affect memory.

Inspect the offered hourly compute price, storage price, upload/download charges, host reliability, available disk, and location. Pick an image with Python 3.12 and Secure Shell access. The pinned PyTorch 2.6.0 environment below targets compatible NVIDIA hardware; a much newer graphics architecture may require a newer, separately tested software environment. Do not choose a card solely by its advertised memory capacity.

2. Create a key in Windows PowerShell

Secure Shell is usually abbreviated SSH. It authenticates a remote connection using a private key kept on your computer and a public key supplied to the host. Never upload the private key to the Vast.ai account page.

powershell
Get-Command ssh, scp, ssh-keygen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh"
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\vast_lab" -C "machine-learning-lab"
Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\vast_lab.pub"

If the key filename already exists, reuse a suitable key or choose a new name; do not overwrite it. Protect the private key with a passphrase. If these commands are missing, install the Windows OpenSSH Client through Settings → System → Optional features, then reopen PowerShell.

Add the displayed public key to your Vast.ai account before creating the instance. Account-key changes are not automatically applied to existing instances. Create the selected instance and wait until it is running. Copy the actual host, port, and username from its Connect instructions.

powershell
$vastHost = Read-Host "Host from Vast Connect"
$vastPort = [int](Read-Host "Port from Vast Connect")
$vastUser = Read-Host "User from Vast Connect"
$vastKey = "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\vast_lab"
ssh -i $vastKey -p $vastPort "${vastUser}@${vastHost}"

These are PowerShell variables, not values to guess. Verify the server fingerprint against provider information when available before accepting a first connection. After connection, the terminal is running the remote Linux shell. Linux commands below run there; Git Bash is not involved.

3. Verify the remote environment and storage

bash
python3 --version
nvidia-smi
pwd
df -h
ls -ld /workspace

Confirm Python 3.12 and that the expected graphics processor is visible. NVIDIA's diagnostic reports the driver and device; it does not prove that your Python package can use the device. We check that separately after installation.

Do not assume that /workspace is a persistent volume. Ordinary container storage survives stopping but is removed when the instance is destroyed. A separately created volume can outlive the instance and continue billing. Vast.ai volumes are tied to the same physical machine; they are not freely attachable to every marketplace host. Inspect the selected template and mount configuration. If you attached a volume at /data, verify it with findmnt -T /data and df -h /data before trusting it.

4. Transfer the course archive

In a second local PowerShell window, set the same four variables from step 2. Change to the directory containing the downloaded ZIP archive. Secure copy, abbreviated SCP, transfers files over Secure Shell; its port option is uppercase -P.

powershell
scp -i $vastKey -P $vastPort .\SML-Lab-Localhost.zip "${vastUser}@${vastHost}:/workspace/"

Back in the remote Linux shell, extract into a new directory, create a virtual environment, and install a graphics-enabled PyTorch package:

bash
python3 -m zipfile -e /workspace/SML-Lab-Localhost.zip /workspace/sml-project
cd /workspace/sml-project/SML-Lab-Localhost
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install torch==2.6.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r lab/requirements.txt -r lab/requirements-foundations.txt
.venv/bin/python lab/lab.py doctor
.venv/bin/python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available()); print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'No graphics processor visible')"

CUDA is NVIDIA's parallel-computing platform, historically named Compute Unified Device Architecture. The cu124 package is built for its 12.4 runtime. A compatible host driver is still required. The final command must print True and the expected device name before a graphics-processor training run. If it prints False, inspect the driver and package installation rather than starting a long experiment.

Do not click the website's fresh local installation option on this prepared cloud environment: that option installs processor-only PyTorch for laptops. The Add foundation packages action preserves the installed PyTorch build.

5. Start the website and private tunnel

In the remote shell:

bash
.venv/bin/python server.py --no-browser

Leave that terminal open. In local PowerShell, with the four connection variables set:

powershell
ssh -i $vastKey -p $vastPort -N -L 127.0.0.1:8766:127.0.0.1:8765 "${vastUser}@${vastHost}"
Start-Process "http://localhost:8766"

The tunnel command occupies its terminal while it runs, so open the browser address manually or run Start-Process from another local PowerShell window. Port 8766 on Windows forwards to port 8765 on the rented machine. Do not enable the server's development-preview flag or expose the code runner on a public network address.

6. Run and compare a neural experiment

In the website's guided terminal:

text
python foundations.py convolution --device cuda --epochs 20 --output outputs/cloud-convolution-01

The explicit device argument selects the graphics processor. Without it, the foundation program defaults to the central processing unit. The tiny included exercise is a connectivity test; overhead can make it slower on a graphics processor. Increase workload only after validating correctness and recording a local comparison. For language-model experiments, use the lesson's actual command with --device cuda where supported and a new output path.

Save the report, measured runtime, actual device, package versions, data settings, and at least one plot. Keep seed, split, and settings the same for a hardware comparison. Explain numerical variation; do not equate faster execution with better predictive quality.

7. Download evidence before cleanup

Stop the web server with Control+C after saving work. From local PowerShell:

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\vast-lab-results
scp -i $vastKey -P $vastPort -r "${vastUser}@${vastHost}:/workspace/sml-project/SML-Lab-Localhost/lab/outputs" .\vast-lab-results

Open a downloaded report and plot to verify the backup. Then stop or destroy the rental in the Vast.ai console according to your retention needs. Closing the browser or Secure Shell session does not stop billing. Stopping can retain billable storage. Destroying the instance deletes its container data; separately retained volumes may still require separate deletion after backup. Review the console for remaining billable resources.

Estimate cost and submit the assessment

Estimate compute hours × compute rate + storage duration × storage rate + transferred data × transfer rate, using the units displayed in your actual offer. As a fictional example only: two hours at $0.40 per hour, storage at $0.01 per hour for those two hours, and two gigabytes transferred at $0.02 per gigabyte total $0.86. This is arithmetic practice, not a current price quote. Persistent storage kept after the experiment changes the total. Account credit is not a guaranteed spending cap.

Submit your local baseline, the rental decision, estimated and actual cost, device checks, remote report, downloaded backup evidence, and cleanup confirmation. If the local experiment already met your goal, submitting the evidence-based decision not to rent satisfies the planning activity.

Troubleshooting and primary documentation

  • Connection refused: compare the running-instance status, address, port, and username with Connect instructions.
  • Permission denied: check the chosen private key and whether its public key was attached before instance creation.
  • Local port busy: choose another local tunnel port; keep the remote target at the server's actual port.
  • Website disconnected: check both the remote server and the local tunnel. Keep their terminals open.
  • Memory exhausted: reduce batch size or sequence length, select a smaller model, and measure again before renting a larger device.

Vast.ai Secure Shell guide, volume behavior, billing questions, and PyTorch version-specific installation.

References for this lesson

Use these sources to check the mechanism and extend the exercise. Research results are not results measured by this lab.

  • Vast.ai: SSH connection guide — Supports SSH-key setup, connection commands and forwarding the localhost lab through an SSH tunnel.
  • Vast.ai: billing — Explains prepaid credits, stopped-instance storage charges and why preserving files and ending billable resources are separate steps.

lessons.title: Prove your engineering decision
lessons.description: Bring evaluation, artifacts and limitations together.
lessons.html:
Lab 34 Complete a defensible capstone

Build a local machine learning support assistant with a bounded scope. Use a tuned classifier for ticket routing and retrieval for troubleshooting facts. Add an explicit unsupported/uncertain route in the application and gather examples that exercise it; the current three-class dataset does not train an abstention category.

Before running final evaluation, write your acceptance criteria. A possible classroom target is at least 90 percent strict schema validity on a substantially enlarged held-out set, improved task accuracy over the base model, and latency within a budget you set after measuring your hardware. These are project goals, not promised results.

DeliverableWhat it proves
Reproducible environment and model revisionAnother engineer can reconstruct the setup
Dataset description, license/origin and split policyYou know what was learned and what was evaluated
Baseline and candidate reports with raw outputsImprovements are observable and failures remain visible
Tests for masks, schemas, retrieval and data boundariesThe surrounding pipeline obeys its contract
Memory, latency and cost measurementsThe system fits its intended environment
Ablation comparisonYou know whether tuning, retrieval or model size drove the change
Model card with limitationsUsers know the intended task and unsupported uses
Reload demonstrationSaved artifacts actually reconstruct the intended model behavior

Suggested ablation: compare untuned/no retrieval, tuned/no retrieval, untuned/retrieval and tuned/retrieval on appropriate separate routing and question-answer tasks. Do not compare classification accuracy directly with freeform question-answering scores as if they measured the same thing.

Oral assessment: explain one successful prediction, one failure and one rejected design change. Trace a prompt from text to token identifiers to embeddings to logits to output. Then trace a training example through loss, gradients, optimizer update and saved adapter.

You are ready for a larger small language model project when you can diagnose whether a failure belongs to data, model capability, retrieval, decoding, dependencies or hardware—and show evidence for that diagnosis.

  • scikit-learn: evaluating estimator performance — Explains the untouched final-test boundary and why tuning after inspecting test results invalidates that boundary.

lessons.title: Pretrained or from scratch: choose the route
lessons.description: Understand checkpoints, training history, reuse, adaptation, and full cost.
lessons.html:
Pretrained models versus building from scratch

Concept — Choose what to reuse, what to learn, and how to prove the choice. Then exercise the decision in Compare pretraining with a fresh start. This chapter applies to image, language, and other neural models. The deep learning workshop explains the numerical learning loop.

What a pretrained model actually contains

An architecture is the computation you design: layers, connections, dimensions, and information flow. Parameters are the numbers learned during training, such as a matrix of weights. A checkpoint saves learned parameter values and enough configuration to restore them. A pretrained model already has learned parameters before your current use or training stage. It may have been trained by someone else, or by you in an earlier experiment.

For text, you usually also need the exact tokenizer, vocabulary, special-token definitions, and prompt format. Loading weights with a different tokenizer can change what every token identifier means. A useful package therefore includes more than a large weight file.

Think of an architecture as a worksheet with adjustable numbers. Random initialization fills the worksheet with small random values; pretraining adjusts those values using examples. Downloading a checkpoint gives you an already adjusted worksheet. It does not give you a reliable database of every original training document.

Base and pretrained are not synonyms. In this language-model context, a base checkpoint usually precedes instruction or preference post-training. An instruction-tuned assistant is also pretrained when you receive it. Pretraining need not use the next-token objective: masked-token prediction, image classification, reconstruction, and other objectives can supply an initial representation.

Five different engineering choices

ChoiceStarting pointWhat changes?Real-world exampleIncluded exercise
Pretrained inferenceExisting learned weightsInput, activations, and output; weights remain fixedRun a local drafting assistantRun your first model
Retrieval-augmented generationExisting generator plus a document collectionRetrieved context and index; ordinary answering does not update generator weightsAnswer questions from current operations notesRetrieval pipeline workshop
Fine-tuningExisting learned weightsSelected original weights or added adaptersLearn a support-triage output formatTeach with a small adapter; transfer comparison
Continued pretrainingExisting learned weightsSelected parameters learn from additional domain dataAdapt language representations to a specialized vocabularyConcept design activity; not a separate production training implementation
Training from scratchNew architecture instance with random weightsTrainable parameters learn their initial useful behaviorBuild a tiny recurrent word predictor or investigate a new architectureDeep, recurrent, masked encoder, encoder–decoder, and original causal-model builds

“From scratch” in these labs means no pretrained model weights. We still use PyTorch for tensor mathematics, automatic differentiation, and standard layers. Implementing matrix multiplication, a graphics-processor kernel, or an entire numerical library is a separate engineering exercise. The counted language model is trained from text counts rather than random neural weights.

How pretraining creates a reusable model

flowchart TD
 D[Permitted training data] --> O[Choose learning objective]
 A[Architecture and random weights] --> T[Predict and measure loss]
 O --> T
 T --> U[Compute gradients and update]
 U --> T
 T --> V[Evaluate on held-out data]
 V --> C[Save pretrained checkpoint]
 C --> I[Use frozen model]
 C --> F[Adapt for a downstream task]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 D[Permitted training data] --> O[Choose learning objective]
 A[Architecture and random weights] --> T[Predict and measure loss]
 O --> T
 T --> U[Compute gradients and update]
 U --> T
 T --> V[Evaluate on held-out data]
 V --> C[Save pretrained checkpoint]
 C --> I[Use frozen model]
 C --> F[Adapt for a downstream task]
  1. Define a useful prediction task and a baseline. A language model may predict a following word; an image model may predict a category.
  2. Obtain permitted data, remove sensitive material, and separate training, validation, and test groups before preprocessing. Near-duplicate documents or photos of the same subject can leak information across naive random splits.
  3. Choose the representation. For language, define tokenization and fit a vocabulary using the permitted training split. For numerical data, fit scaling only on training examples.
  4. Define the architecture and initialize its trainable values. Random does not mean arbitrary magnitude: initialization is chosen to keep computations well behaved.
  5. Run a forward pass, measure a loss, calculate gradients, and take an optimizer step. Repeat with training examples.
  6. Use validation to choose settings. After selection, evaluate on untouched test examples that did not drive those choices.
  7. Save the model, configuration, preprocessing, revision, settings, and metrics. Reconstruct it in a new model instance and verify a prediction.
  8. Reuse the checkpoint directly or adapt it for another objective. The first stage is now pretraining relative to the second.

A network starts without useful learned task knowledge, not without structure. Architecture and training data encode choices made by its engineers. A tiny training run demonstrates this process but does not produce the breadth of a general assistant.

Understand the training target

For next-token prediction, the text supplies its own targets. With “please restart amber,” the input “please restart” has the next-word target “amber.” This is self-supervised learning: targets are constructed from the data rather than manually supplied for each prediction. For masked-token prediction, hide a word and predict the original. For supervised intent classification, supply a category such as “restart.”

If the correct token receives probability 0.1, its negative natural logarithm is approximately 2.303. If the probability rises to 0.8, the loss becomes approximately 0.223. A lower loss means better probability assignment under that objective. It does not establish factual accuracy or correct tool execution.

Choose a route using evidence

flowchart TD
 P[Define task and success metric] --> E{Suitable pretrained model?}
 E -->|Yes| B[Measure a frozen baseline]
 E -->|No| S[Small scratch feasibility run]
 B --> K{Missing current knowledge?}
 K -->|Yes| R[Evaluate retrieval]
 K -->|No| A[Evaluate targeted adaptation]
 S --> C[Compare quality and full cost]
 R --> C
 A --> C
 C --> D[Choose and monitor the system]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 P[Define task and success metric] --> E{Suitable pretrained model?}
 E -->|Yes| B[Measure a frozen baseline]
 E -->|No| S[Small scratch feasibility run]
 B --> K{Missing current knowledge?}
 K -->|Yes| R[Evaluate retrieval]
 K -->|No| A[Evaluate targeted adaptation]
 S --> C[Compare quality and full cost]
 R --> C
 A --> C
 C --> D[Choose and monitor the system]

Use a pretrained baseline when the checkpoint supports your inputs, output needs, license, and hardware. Consider adaptation when representative failures show a behavior or domain gap. Consider retrieval when answers must refer to a changing document collection. Consider scratch training for teaching, architecture research, unusual input representations, or a justified task/data/compute requirement. Retrieval and adaptation can also be combined.

Cost comparison: count pretraining, adaptation, data work, evaluation, serving, and maintenance separately. In the included transfer experiment, the pretrained branch gets 300 extra learning updates before both branches receive the same downstream examples and 80 adaptation updates. It would be misleading to call that equal total training compute. A frozen encoder still performs forward computation and occupies memory.

Start on the central processing unit. Every new build in this release is deliberately tiny and was executed locally. No Vast.ai rental is required. For an expanded experiment, first measure memory and elapsed time, then follow the existing Vast.ai procedure, set a spending limit, save artifacts, and inspect remaining billable resources. Do not infer a production foundation-model budget from these tiny runs.

Start-to-finish assessment: an operations assistant

Define the problem as mapping a permitted operations request to a small category set. Write the success criterion before choosing a model: category accuracy, unsupported-input behavior, and inference latency. Describe the input text contract, label definitions, training data rights, and document/group split. Compare a simple baseline, random initialization, pretrained fine-tuning, and a frozen representation. Preserve exactly the same downstream training examples and evaluation set across the neural branches.

Save and reload the selected model with its vocabulary and category order. Submit predictions for new requests and for out-of-domain text. Deploy the prototype only through the local input interface. Production would need broader data, authorization outside the model, calibration, drift monitoring, failure handling, and a versioned rollback artifact. A predicted action must not automatically become an executed operation.

Evidence to submit: your decision table, data/split contract, measured branch results, full compute accounting, one failure, saved-model prediction, and a reason to revisit the choice later. A lower score after pretraining is a valid finding. Do not tune away inconvenient results without reporting the changed conditions.

Explanation checks: Can you pretrain your own model? Yes. Does fine-tuning create a model with no prior training? No. Does retrieval train the generator during ordinary answering? No. Is deep learning limited to language models? No; the course's image, graph, and reconstruction networks also use neural representations.

Primary reading

  • PyTorch transfer learning tutorial: fine-tuning and frozen feature extraction.
  • Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers: masked-language pretraining and downstream adaptation.
  • Automatic differentiation with PyTorch: gradients and parameter updates.

References for this lesson

  • PyTorch — Automatic differentiation — Connect the forward computation, gradient calculation and optimizer update to the runnable training loop.
  • LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models — Hu et al. (2021) — Primary source for learning low-rank updates while freezing pretrained weights.
