lab-workflow.title: Run, compare, save, and explain
lab-workflow.html:
Run, compare, save, and explain an experiment

This is the shared operating guide for the local workbench. Each lesson supplies its own model, data contract, comparison, and assessment. Use the procedure that fits that lesson's scope.

Start with the lesson's scope

ScopeWhat you actually produceWhat you must not claim
Concept activityA design, calculation, or critiqueThat a model was trained
Numerical mechanism demonstrationIntermediate values, errors, gradients, or memory calculationsA deployable trained checkpoint
Pretrained inferenceOutputs from existing weights and measured evaluationTraining a foundation model
AdaptationUpdated parameters or an adapter, with its required base modelA new model trained from random weights
Training from random weightsA tiny fitted model and its evaluation artifactsProduction quality from a teaching dataset
Retrieval experimentAn index, retrieved evidence, and optionally generated answersGenerator training during ordinary retrieval

Run a command in the correct place

The Practice buttons and guided terminal run the listed programs from the bundled lab folder, using the configured Python environment. Install packages through Package setup when required. Keep an existing working environment rather than recreating it for each lesson.

For an external Windows terminal, start in the extracted folder containing server.py, then enter lab. These examples assume the environment is .venv in the project root; substitute the interpreter you configured if different.

powershell
Push-Location .\lab
& ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\foundations.py linear --output outputs\linear-NEW
Pop-Location
bat
pushd lab
..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe foundations.py linear --output outputs\linear-NEW
popd

Use the command belonging to your lesson. Replace NEW with a unique name. Practice buttons replace {run} automatically; a normal terminal does not. Experiments refuse to overwrite an existing nonempty output folder so earlier evidence survives.

Decide what the comparison means

Write down the question before running. Keep the data, split, and seed fixed when changing one setting. A configured reference run is a comparison baseline; it is not necessarily a majority-class, mean-prediction, or random-policy baseline. Claim a built-in baseline only when the lesson and report actually include one. If a stronger baseline is a design activity, implement and identify it separately.

For ordinary train/validation/test experiments, fit preprocessing and parameters on training data, select settings using validation, and reserve the final test. Repeatedly choosing settings after viewing the test turns it into selection data.

Some lessons have different protocols. A fixed-graph experiment evaluates unseen labels on the same visible graph. A small adversarial generator is assessed on fresh simulator draws. A grid policy is assessed in the same environment. These results must not be renamed independent test sets or evidence of generalization to new populations. Follow the protocol stated in that lesson and report.

Inspect actual evidence

For experiments that save report.json, read the dataset description, selected protocol, settings, metrics, limitations, and artifact paths. A training loss is an optimization signal; the lesson's evaluation explains useful performance. Model quality, latency, memory, and cost are separate measurements. Preserve failures and raw outputs.

Plots written by the program are results from that run. Diagrams inside lessons are teaching illustrations unless explicitly labeled as recorded results. A conceptual diagram is not an activation trace or a performance benchmark.

Save, reload, and predict

Where supported, a successful run creates a model manifest, example input, learned state, and report. In Practice, choose Load saved example, edit values while respecting the lesson's shape and units, then choose Predict new input. The page remembers the successful folder by stable lesson ID.

The command-line alternative below applies to models supported by predict_saved.py. Replace both placeholders with your actual paths; run it from lab using the same interpreter as training.

text
python predict_saved.py --model-dir outputs/MODEL-FOLDER --input outputs/MODEL-FOLDER/example-input.json --output outputs/prediction-NEW.json

A mechanism-only exercise may have no saved model. Language-model adapters require their matching base revision and tokenizer. The original scratch-model checkpoint uses its own loader. Only load model artifacts you created or trust, and preserve the architecture and preprocessing needed to interpret their state.

Keep local prototypes and production claims distinct

The local workbench runs with your account's permissions. A shared service requires its own input validation, authentication, authorization, request limits, monitoring, versioning, rollback, and rejection behavior. Each lesson names the task-specific risks to monitor. A synthetic-data score does not establish real-world performance.

Start on the local central processing unit for these tiny exercises. Estimate memory and runtime before using optional graphics-processor instructions. Keep costs for data, training, inference, retained storage, and verification separate.

Submit assessable work

Use the lesson's specific evidence checklist. Include your prediction before the experiment, actual measurements, a relevant comparison, one failure or limitation, and an explanation of whether the intended requirement was met. Include save/reload and new-input evidence only for exercises that implement them. Notes and progress remain associated with the browser profile and exact localhost address.

Shared references

  • scikit-learn: common pitfalls — preprocessing, leakage, and consistent transformations.
  • PyTorch: saving and loading models — state dictionaries and reconstructing model instances.
  • Python: virtual environments — project environments and interpreter paths.

build-plans.title: More model build plans
build-plans.html:
Additional model build plans

Concept — These are complete project plans and design activities. These larger task-specific plans remain design activities. Small runnable language-model variants now appear in Build and retrieve: a recurrent word predictor, masked-token encoder, and recurrent encoder–decoder. Those exercises do not implement every task specified below; diffusion generation remains Concept only. The language-model atlas explains their algorithms; the plans here connect them to practical deliverables. Use the 18 runnable foundation builds to practice the shared engineering workflow first.

Recurrent networks: forecast a sensor stream

Problem: predict the next reading from a recent sequence. A recurrent neural network updates a hidden state at every time step. A long short-term memory network adds gates and a separate cell state; a gated recurrent unit uses a different gated update. Gates control information flow, rather than guaranteeing unlimited memory.

Start-to-finish build: collect permitted timestamped sensor readings; resolve missing intervals without using future values; split chronologically before constructing overlapping windows; fit scaling on training measurements; compare with predicting the last observed value; build a small recurrent layer and numeric output head; optimize prediction loss; validate on later time periods; evaluate once on the final period; save weights, architecture, scaling, window length, and time-zone assumptions; reload to predict an unseen sequence; deploy a bounded local endpoint; monitor error, missing readings, and sensor replacement.

Algorithm exercise: start a scalar state at zero. Apply state = 0.5 * state + input to [2, 0, 0, 3]. Obtain [2, 1, 0.5, 3.25]. Change the multiplier to 0.9 and explain the longer memory. Run the workbench's state example. This is a memory-mechanism exercise, not trained long short-term memory.

Assessment: draw the window/target boundary; demonstrate why adjacent overlapping windows randomly split across datasets leak information; specify expected input shape [batch, time, features]; propose a last-value baseline and a failure case. A tiny training extension should fit locally. Rent a graphics processor only for substantially larger sequence workloads.

Primary reference: PyTorch long short-term memory layer.

Encoder models: classify a support request

Problem: assign a ticket category using the whole request. An encoder forms contextual representations of the input; a small classification head turns the representation into category scores. Bidirectional context is useful because a word can be interpreted using text on both sides. This is different from predicting future text with a causal mask.

Start-to-finish build: define a category guide and collect permitted, independently labeled tickets; group duplicates and related threads; split by thread and time; select a compact pretrained encoder and pin its revision; tokenize with its matching tokenizer; train a classification head or fine-tune selected layers; compare with a keyword or linear baseline; select confidence/rejection rules using validation; test class recall and calibration; save model, tokenizer, label mapping, maximum length, and preprocessing; reload for one new ticket; serve locally; monitor category drift and requests outside the label set.

Design exercise: label ten fictional tickets using your category guide, including ambiguous and multi-topic examples. Write the rule for an unknown category and draw where human review occurs. Explain why a similarity embedding objective is not automatically supplied by a classification-trained encoder.

Assessment: supply the labeling guide, duplicate-group split, input/output contract, baseline, error-cost table, model version plan, and drift response. Fine-tuning a small encoder can begin locally; larger datasets may justify a graphics processor.

Primary reference: sequence classification.

Encoder–decoder models: summarize a maintenance report

Problem: produce a short report summary while preserving dates, actions, and unresolved issues. An encoder reads the source; a decoder generates the summary using previous output tokens and cross-attention to encoded source information.

flowchart TD
 A[Source report] --> B[Tokenizer and encoder]
 C[Earlier output tokens] --> D[Causal decoder]
 B -->|Cross-attention| D
 D --> E[Next-token probabilities]
 E --> F{End token or limit}
 F -->|Continue| C
 F -->|Finish| G[Summary and factual checks]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Source report] --> B[Tokenizer and encoder]
 C[Earlier output tokens] --> D[Causal decoder]
 B -->|Cross-attention| D
 D --> E[Next-token probabilities]
 E --> F{End token or limit}
 F -->|Continue| C
 F -->|Finish| G[Summary and factual checks]

Start-to-finish build: obtain permitted report/summary pairs; remove duplicate reports across splits; write a factuality rubric; choose a compact encoder–decoder checkpoint; tokenize source and target separately; mask padded target positions in the loss; fine-tune on training pairs using teacher forcing; validate generated summaries rather than only teacher-forced loss; compare with extracting the opening sentences; assess factual omissions and invented details on final test; save tokenizer and generation settings with weights; reload and summarize a new report; deploy with source-length and output-length limits; monitor changes in report format and factual-error rates.

Design exercise: write a three-sentence maintenance report and a one-sentence reference summary. Mark every summary claim with the source sentence that supports it. Then construct a fluent but incorrect summary and explain why word overlap alone can miss its error. Explain why teacher forcing supplies prior target tokens during training, while generation uses its own earlier outputs.

Assessment: paired-data schema, train/validation/test policy, factuality rubric, generated examples, length limits, artifact manifest, and rollback plan. Begin with a small checkpoint and few examples; rent only after measuring memory and runtime.

Primary reference: summarization workflow.

Diffusion models: generate small visual patterns

Problem: generate diverse, permitted texture patterns for a simulator. A diffusion model learns to reverse a specified corruption process. A common continuous-data setup trains a network to predict added noise at a sampled noise level, then repeatedly applies a compatible reverse update during generation. The sampler and noise schedule are part of the model system.

Start-to-finish build: obtain licensed small images and split by source asset; normalize pixels; define a noise schedule; sample a time step and noise for each training example; combine the clean image and noise; supply the corrupted image and time embedding to a small denoiser; train noise prediction; evaluate held-out denoising and generated sample diversity; save weights, normalization, schedule, and sampler configuration; reload; start from noise and generate through reverse steps; inspect duplicates and missing modes; serve locally with bounded resolution and step count; monitor runtime and failure patterns. Larger visual diffusion training often justifies rented graphics hardware, while a tiny numerical corruption exercise does not.

Numerical exercise: use the simplified corruption formula noisy = sqrt(alpha) * clean + sqrt(1-alpha) * noise. For clean value 2, alpha 0.64, and noise -1, the result is 0.8 * 2 + 0.6 * -1 = 1. Explain why the denoiser also needs to know the noise level. This arithmetic does not implement a trained reverse sampler.

Distinction: a one-pass denoising autoencoder is not automatically a diffusion generator. Discrete text diffusion needs its own token-corruption and generation formulation; do not apply a continuous-image sampler directly to integer token identifiers. The language-model atlas contains a masked-token conceptual algorithm.

Assessment: write the corruption and reverse-sampling interfaces, identify which tensors are targets, specify a diversity check, and list every artifact needed to reproduce a sample. Mark the sampler implementation and training as planned work until tested.

Primary reference: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.

Learning strategies that cut across these families

Concept — Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples; self-training can add high-confidence pseudo-labels, but bad pseudo-labels can reinforce errors. Contrastive learning trains representations to distinguish related from unrelated examples; the choice of pairs defines what similarity means. Online learning updates as examples arrive; evaluation must respect time and changing data. Transfer learning starts from learned parameters rather than random initialization. These strategies can use multiple model architectures.

Design activity: for the support-ticket project, specify which examples are labeled, how you would prevent held-out tickets from entering pseudo-label training, what makes a valid positive pair, and how an online evaluation would work before accepting an update. No additional strategy is implemented merely because it appears in this plan.

ml-atlas.title: Machine learning atlas
ml-atlas.html:
The broader machine learning atlas

This atlas maps the areas implemented in this course. It is not a claim to enumerate every research architecture. Model mechanisms, learning signals, tasks, and deployment techniques overlap. A graph network can learn from supervised targets; a Transformer can learn from self-supervised targets and later from rewards.

Language models are machine-learning models. The Foundations and Language models tracks are two learning paths within the same field. Count-based word predictors learn from data without neural networks; modern neural language models usually use deep learning. Language modeling describes what is modeled, while a Transformer describes how computation works.

Open the Language model atlas for the full explanation, algorithms, overlapping design choices, and a classification exercise. A classifier that labels messages as spam is also machine learning, but a spam label alone does not make it a language model. Natural language processing is the broader application area for working with human language.

Coverage you can verify

Concept means a guided explanation, diagram, decision exercise, and comprehension check. Runnable implementation lab means the package includes executable code and a practice action. The scope text explains whether it is a small mechanism demonstration, evaluation of a pretrained model, or actual training. No label claims production readiness.

TopicStatusWhat you will do
Linear regression: learn a weighted predictionRunnable implementation labPredict a number, understand each coefficient, and beat a simple baseline.
Logistic regression: turn scores into probabilitiesRunnable implementation labLearn classification, thresholds, class imbalance, and confusion matrices.
Decision trees: inspect the questionsRunnable implementation labBuild a branching classifier and see the cost of increasing depth.
Ensembles: compare forests and boostingRunnable implementation labCombine learners, compare the actual results, and distinguish two different strategies.
Nearest neighbors: classify by similarityRunnable implementation labObserve how a distance rule and neighbor count reshape a decision boundary.
Kernel methods: learn a curved boundaryRunnable implementation labCompare a linear support vector machine with a nonlinear similarity kernel.
Naive Bayes: combine evidence with probabilitiesRunnable implementation labBuild a probability-based classifier and inspect its independence assumption.
Gaussian processes: predict with uncertaintyRunnable implementation labFit a smooth function and inspect an uncertainty band beyond observed inputs.
Clustering: discover groups without supplied labelsRunnable implementation labCompare centroid-based groups with density-based exploration.
Principal component analysis: compress measurementsRunnable implementation labReduce 64 pixel measurements to fewer coordinates and reconstruct the images.
Dense neural networks: train a hidden representationRunnable implementation labBuild a small multilayer perceptron and inspect gradients, shape, and loss.
Convolutional networks: share a visual detectorRunnable implementation labTrain spatial filters, follow tensor shapes, and compare with a dense network.
Graph neural networks: learn from connectionsRunnable implementation labCombine node features with neighborhood information and test an edge-removal ablation.
Autoencoders: reconstruct through a bottleneckRunnable implementation labLearn a compact representation and reconstruct clean inputs from noisy observations.
Variational autoencoders: learn a distributionRunnable implementation labAdd probabilistic latent variables and balance reconstruction with regularization.
Adversarial generation: train two competing modelsRunnable implementation labWatch a generator learn a two-mode distribution and diagnose mode collapse.
Statistical language models: count before you train a networkRunnable implementation labBuild an inspectable word predictor with counts, smoothing, and perplexity.
Reinforcement learning: learn actions from rewardsRunnable implementation labTrain a complete small action-value learner and compare it with random behavior.

The earlier language-model track retains its dense Transformer, mixture-of-experts, state-space, and hybrid implementations. The Build and retrieve track adds runnable recurrent language modeling, masked-token encoder pretraining, and recurrent encoder–decoder training from random weights. It also adds a pretrained-versus-scratch comparison and retrieval evaluation with actual frozen generation. Diffusion-language modeling remains Concept material without a standalone training implementation. Coding and vision lessons run pretrained models; they do not train production code or vision-language models from scratch.

Compare model mechanisms and evaluation tasks

These overview graphics compare several methods. For a worked example of one method, open its individual lesson.

A compact map of modeling choices

flowchart TD
 A[Predict from examples] --> B[Weighted or probabilistic relationships]
 A --> C[Partitions or similarity]
 A --> D[Learned neural representations]
 B --> E[Linear models and Gaussian processes]
 C --> F[Trees and nearest neighbors]
 D --> G[Dense and convolutional networks]
 D --> H[Graphs and sequence models]
 I[Choose a training signal] --> A
 J[Define the deployment task] --> A
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 A[Predict from examples] --> B[Weighted or probabilistic relationships]
 A --> C[Partitions or similarity]
 A --> D[Learned neural representations]
 B --> E[Linear models and Gaussian processes]
 C --> F[Trees and nearest neighbors]

The drawing is a teaching map of representative choices, not an exclusive mathematical taxonomy. Unsupervised methods and generative objectives introduce additional choices described in the modules below.

windows.title: Windows installation
windows.html:
> CURRENT WINDOWS CPU UPDATE — Python 3.12. Read [SECURITY-TESTING.md](SECURITY-TESTING.md) first. Use a new folder and its own environment on localhost port 8766. Earlier platform and dependency recipes below are historical; use the hashed Windows lock for this candidate. Pretrained language/vision and GPU compatibility are not yet certified.

Run Machine Learning Super Lab on Windows

Use PowerShell or Command Prompt. Git Bash, Git, Node.js, and a cloud account are not required. The browser site runs actual Python programs on your computer; it is not an isolated virtual machine.

1. Install Python 3.12

Open PowerShell from Start and run:

powershell
winget install --exact --id Python.Python.3.12 --source winget --scope user

Let installation finish. Close the entire terminal application and open PowerShell again. The course uses Python 3.12 for compatibility with its pinned package versions.

2. Find Python without depending on the launcher

The py command is a separate launcher. If it is missing, Python may still be installed. These PowerShell commands find common installation locations:

powershell
$python312 = @(
    "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Python\Python312\python.exe"
    "$env:ProgramFiles\Python312\python.exe"
) | Where-Object { Test-Path $_ } | Select-Object -First 1

if ($python312) {
    & $python312 --version
} else {
    winget list --exact --id Python.Python.3.12
}

Expected: Python 3.12.x. The ampersand tells PowerShell to execute the program at the quoted path. The variable lasts only in this PowerShell session.

If Python appears in the package list but neither path exists, check Settings → Apps → Installed apps for Python 3.12, and use its actual installation path. To inspect executable commands available on your search path:

powershell
Get-Command python, python3, py -All -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If no installed package is found, run step 1 and check its full output. If winget is missing, install or update Microsoft's App Installer from the Microsoft Store, reopen PowerShell, and retry. Alternatively use the official Python installer linked below. For the classic Python installer, select 64-bit Python 3.12, include the launcher, and select “Add python.exe to PATH.”

3. Extract and launch the website

Download SML-Lab-Localhost.zip. In File Explorer, right-click it → Extract All. Open the extracted SML-Lab-Localhost folder and double-click start-lab.cmd.

The launcher checks the Python launcher, common direct executable paths, then the python command. Keep its window open. It opens:

http://localhost:8765

If the browser does not open, enter that address yourself. This address works after the server starts on your own computer.

Launch from PowerShell instead

Change the example folder to the location containing server.py:

powershell
Set-Location "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\SML-Lab-Localhost\SML-Lab-Localhost"
.\start-lab.cmd

If you extracted directly to Downloads, the folder might instead be Downloads\SML-Lab-Localhost. Verify with Get-ChildItem; server.py and start-lab.cmd must appear. With a custom Python location:

powershell
$python312 = "C:\your\actual\Python312\python.exe"
& $python312 .\server.py

Launch from Command Prompt instead

bat
cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\Downloads\SML-Lab-Localhost\SML-Lab-Localhost"
start-lab.cmd

The same extraction-path rule applies. To use a common direct Python path in Command Prompt:

bat
"%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\Python312\python.exe" server.py

4. Install the machine learning packages from the website

Browser users: complete Lesson 21 — Build your workspace — first. Open Practice → Install local packages and wait for SUCCEEDED. Setup creates a fresh .lab-environments/env-... environment, installs the hash-pinned Windows CPU packages, validates them and selects the runtime through .runtime-python. Normal Downloads paths are supported, and existing environments are preserved. This downloads several hundred megabytes or more; watch the actual console log.

Run the environment diagnostic. Then return to Foundations Lesson 1 or your chosen learning path. Model weights download separately on first use. The first workbench example uses only built-in Python and can run before package installation.

No PowerShell activation script is needed. No execution-policy change is needed.

Manual package installation if preferred

From the folder containing server.py, use the same setup helper as the browser:

powershell
py -3.12 lab/setup_environment.py
$labPython = (Get-Content .runtime-python -Raw).Trim()
& $labPython -m pip check

In Command Prompt:

bat
py -3.12 lab\setup_environment.py
if errorlevel 1 exit /b 1
start-lab.cmd

If py is unavailable, replace it with the verified Python 3.12 executable described above. Setup never needs an administrator or an execution-policy change.

Upgrade an existing working installation

Extract into a new folder and keep the old folder, environment, learner inputs/outputs, run logs and notes. For the updated dependencies, use Lesson 21 or the setup helper to create a fresh environment rather than modifying a working one in place. For side-by-side testing use start-security-test.cmd and http://localhost:8766. Read [SECURITY-TESTING.md](SECURITY-TESTING.md) for exact backup, promotion, restart and rollback commands.

Browser progress belongs to the browser profile and exact origin. Keep http://localhost:8765 when you eventually switch copies; do not clear its storage. Port 8766 has separate progress. Copy learner files only into empty destinations and keep the originals.

Troubleshooting

For the synthetic-data addition, open Build and retrieve → Synthetic data: generate, audit, and compare (lesson 42). The same environment and foundation packages work; no new package family is required. Run the four Practice comparisons, load the saved example, and inspect the plots in Experiment results. The synthetic-data reference is also in the sidebar.

  • py is not recognized: use the direct executable or the included launcher. Installing the separate launcher is optional.
  • python opens Microsoft Store: that command may resolve to Windows' shortcut. Use the direct executable. Disabling a shortcut does not install Python.
  • Port 8765 is already in use: first check whether the lab is already running. To select another port: & $python312 .\server.py --port 8766, then open http://localhost:8766.
  • Missing package: install local packages inside the website, then run the diagnostic again. The website uses the project environment automatically.
  • Package download fails: keep the full terminal log. Check internet access and available disk space. Retry package setup; package installation can reuse downloads.
  • Close the lab: save logs you need, then press Control+C in the launcher window. Stopping a job can leave partial output; start a new training run with a new output folder.
  • Custom Python path: provide it explicitly as shown above; do not paste a guessed path.

Official references:

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/python/beginners
  • https://docs.python.org/3.12/using/windows.html
  • https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-31210/ (classic installer; later Python 3.12 security releases also exist)
  • https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs/tree/master/manifests/p/Python/Python/3/12

foundations.title: Start with the concepts
foundations.html:
Before the laboratories build an accurate mental model

An algorithm is a sequence of steps for carrying out a task. A model architecture specifies how information passes through mathematical operations. A training algorithm adjusts the model's learned numbers. A trained checkpoint contains the resulting numbers and the information needed to load them. A software application connects the model to inputs, retrieval, permissions and outputs. These are related components, but they are not the same object.

For example, a recipe describes a procedure, while the current settings of an adjustable oven describe part of the system's state. In a neural network, the architecture and training procedure are specified by code; training learns many numerical settings. Those settings are called parameters. The analogy helps distinguish the procedure from the learned values, but a language model does not literally store a collection of recipes or reason like a human chef.

The first ten concepts with concrete examples

ConceptPlain meaningExampleWhat it does not mean
ParameterA learned number that affects the computationA value in a matrix that transforms one representation into anotherA separate fact or a whole stored sentence
WeightUsually a learned multiplier; often used informally for all model parametersMultiplying an input feature by 0.3A human-written rule such as “always choose memory”
TokenOne unit of the model's vocabularyA word fragment, punctuation mark or byte, depending on the tokenizerNecessarily a full word
VocabularyThe set of tokens a tokenizer recognizesAn indexed list of permitted token piecesA list of everything the model knows
Token identifierAn integer used to look up a tokenThe integer 17 might refer to a particular tokenA quantity whose numerical order measures meaning
EmbeddingA learned vector associated with an input itemToken 17 is mapped to a list of hundreds of numbersA simple dictionary definition or an independently labeled “meaning axis”
ActivationA temporary computed value during one model runA representation after the third layer processes this promptA permanently changed learned weight
ContextInformation available to this predictionThe prompt and previously generated tokensEverything the model has ever seen in previous sessions
LogitA raw score before normalization into probabilitiesScores of 3.0, 1.0 and -2.0 for three candidate tokensA probability, confidence guarantee or truth score
CheckpointSaved model state and configurationA weight file plus architecture settingsA complete reproducible application without its dependencies and tokenizer

The key contrast is between learned parameters, which usually stay fixed during inference, and activations, which change as the model processes new input. Inference means using a trained model. Training means calculating a learning signal and updating selected parameters.

Follow one sentence through a language model

Suppose the prompt is “The cat sat on the”. The following numbers are invented to explain the process; they are not measurements from our selected checkpoint.

  1. Tokenize the text. A hypothetical tokenizer might produce ['The', ' cat', ' sat', ' on', ' the']. Another tokenizer could split these pieces differently. Leading spaces can be part of a token.
  2. Look up identifiers. The pieces might become [12, 48, 305, 27, 9]. These numbers are vocabulary addresses, not semantic measurements.
  3. Look up embeddings. Each identifier selects a vector of learned numbers. This is similar to looking up a row in a table, but the row contains learned features rather than prose.
  4. Process the sequence. Layers transform the vectors. A Transformer uses attention to combine information from permitted positions. Other architectures may update a compact state instead.
  5. Produce scores. The last position produces one logit for each vocabulary token.
  6. Normalize the scores. A softmax operation turns the logits into nonnegative probabilities that sum to one across the vocabulary.
  7. Choose a token. A decoding rule might select the most probable token or sample according to the probabilities.
  8. Append and repeat. If the chosen token is ' mat', the next prediction sees the original prompt plus that token. Generation stops at an end marker, a length limit or another stopping rule.

An illustrative probability table could be:

Candidate next tokenIllustrative probability
mat0.55
floor0.25
chair0.10
All other tokens combined0.10

Choosing the highest-probability token gives mat. Sampling could produce floor. Neither operation verifies whether a real cat sat anywhere. A language model predicts tokens; an application must add the appropriate evidence and checks for its task.

Check yourself: if you ask the same model a new question, which changes: the prompt, the activations or the learned weights? In ordinary inference, the first two change; the weights do not.

A small model is small in capacity not in conceptual complexity

A model advertised as 135 million parameters contains roughly that many learned numerical values. It does not contain 135 million facts. Parameter count is one resource indicator. Data quality, training methods, architecture, context length and task fit also affect performance.

The core course uses a 135-million-parameter pretrained model for useful experiments and a roughly 137-thousand-parameter toy model for seeing training mechanics. The toy model is much smaller than the approximate small-language-model range used in this course. It is an educational microscope, not a competing assistant.

A larger model can still fail at a task with poor instructions or bad retrieval. A smaller model may perform well on a narrow, clearly defined task. We choose size using measured task quality and resource requirements rather than assuming that every problem needs the largest available model.

Understand memory before renting a machine

The central processing unit is the computer's general-purpose processor. The graphics processing unit performs many suitable mathematical operations in parallel. Random-access memory is the computer's working memory. A dedicated graphics card has its own device memory, often called video random-access memory. Disk storage holds files when the program is not using them.

Imagine a workshop. Disk is the storage cupboard; system memory is a workbench; device memory is the workbench next to a specialized machine. A component in the cupboard does not automatically fit on either workbench. Likewise, successfully downloading a model does not prove it will fit during inference or training.

Use this planning equation:

total runtime memory = weights + activations + cached context + temporary buffers + framework overhead

During training, also account for gradients and optimizer state. A gradient is a derivative describing how a change would affect loss. Optimizer state is extra numerical history used by the update algorithm. Compressing the weights reduces one part of the total, not necessarily every part.

A decision algorithm for choosing a starting model

This is a practical decision procedure, not a claim that the categories are mutually exclusive. First select a task and output contract. Then choose an architecture or checkpoint. Apply training and deployment choices afterward.

  1. Write the required output. Is it a label, a search ranking, generated text, a code change or an answer about an image?
  2. Try the simplest suitable baseline. Labels or ranking may need only rules or an encoder. Generated text usually makes a dense instruction-tuned Transformer a reasonable beginner choice. Images require an image-capable model.
  3. Check the input requirements. A text-only model cannot inspect pixels merely because a filename appears in its prompt.
  4. Estimate and then measure memory. Include context, activations and runtime overhead, not just the model download size.
  5. Measure the baseline on examples excluded from training. Define correctness before examining candidate outputs.
  6. Diagnose the dominant failure. Missing external facts suggest retrieval. Wrong response behavior may suggest better training data. Memory exhaustion suggests a smaller checkpoint, shorter context or a suitable compression approach. Incorrect reasoning may require better data, verification or a more capable model.
  7. Change one thing. Repeat the evaluation under comparable conditions and keep the change only if the evidence supports it.
  8. Explore advanced architectures when you have a reason. Study a mixture of experts for routing and capacity tradeoffs, or state space and hybrid models for sequence-processing tradeoffs. Do not assume either is automatically faster or better.

For our first project, the task is to generate a small structured answer classifying a support ticket. We use a dense instruction-tuned Transformer because its tooling is straightforward and its training behavior is easy to inspect. A conventional classifier is also a valid baseline for this task.

The learning algorithm explained slowly

Using the model

Inference takes an input, computes predictions using learned weights and returns an output. A conversation can maintain history in the prompt or application state. That is not the same as updating weights.

Teaching the model

Training adds a correct target and a method for adjusting selected weights:

  1. Read a training example, including the input and desired output.
  2. Calculate the model's predictions with the current parameters.
  3. Calculate a loss, a number that measures a defined aspect of prediction error.
  4. Use backpropagation to calculate how the loss depends on trainable parameters.
  5. Use an optimizer to update those parameters.
  6. Repeat over training examples and periodically measure performance on validation examples that do not update the weights.
  7. After choosing your settings, evaluate on a final test set that was not used for those choices.

For next-token learning, a common loss is the negative natural logarithm of the probability assigned to the correct token. If that probability is 0.1, the loss is about 2.303. If it rises to 0.8, the loss falls to about 0.223. Lower token loss means the correct tokens receive more probability under that measurement; it does not automatically prove factual accuracy, good formatting or application success.

A numerical gradient update

Consider the toy predictor prediction = weight × input. Let input be 2, target be 6 and current weight be 1. The prediction is 2. Define squared-error loss as (prediction - target)^2, giving 16.

The derivative of this loss with respect to the weight is 2 × (prediction - target) × input, which is -16. With a learning rate of 0.1, gradient descent updates the weight to 1 - 0.1 × (-16) = 2.6. The new prediction is 5.2 and the new loss is 0.64.

The gradient described a local slope. The learning rate controlled the step size. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute such derivatives through many connected operations. This one-number exercise explains the mechanism without pretending that a language model has a simple convex optimization landscape.

Mini exercise: redo the same update with learning rate 1.0. The weight becomes 17, the prediction becomes 34 and the loss becomes 784. A larger step was worse. This is why changing a learning rate is an engineering experiment rather than a guarantee of faster learning.

Training words that often get confused

WordExact meaning in this courseCommon mistake
BatchThe examples processed together for a forward/backward calculationAssuming batch size means context length
Sequence lengthThe number of token positions in an exampleAssuming it equals the number of words
Optimizer stepOne update of trainable parametersCalling every step an epoch
EpochOne complete pass through the defined training dataset under an epoch-based scheduleCalling 60 randomly sampled updates 60 full passes
Learning rateScale used by the optimizer's update ruleTreating it as a measure of model intelligence
Gradient accumulationCollecting gradients across multiple smaller batches before an updateAssuming it removes the memory required by one individual example
OverfittingLearning training-specific patterns that fail to generalizeConcluding that low training loss guarantees success
Data leakageLetting information from evaluation influence training or selection improperlySplitting nearly identical copies into separate sets and calling them independent
HyperparameterA chosen training or system setting, such as rank or learning rateConfusing it with a weight learned by the optimizer
Random seedAn input controlling a pseudorandom sequenceAssuming the same seed guarantees identical behavior on every device and software version

Adaptation changes different parts of the system

MethodPlain algorithmWhich learned weights change?
Pretraining from scratchInitialize a model; learn token patterns from a corpusThe selected model parameters begin without useful pretrained knowledge and are trained
Continued pretrainingStart from a checkpoint; continue learning from domain textThe chosen trainable parameters
Full supervised fine-tuningTrain on requests and desired answersAll or most chosen original parameters
Low-rank adaptationAdd small trainable matrix pairs to selected transformationsAdded adapter parameters; most original parameters remain frozen
Quantized low-rank adaptationKeep a compressed base and train added adaptersAdapter parameters; the quantized base remains frozen in the intended setup
DistillationLet a teacher produce training signals; train a student to reproduce useful behaviorStudent parameters selected for training
Retrieval-augmented generationFind relevant evidence; insert it into the prompt; generate an answerNone in the ordinary retrieval-and-inference operation

For low-rank adaptation, a large matrix update is represented using the product of two smaller matrices. If the original transformation maps 576 input features to 576 outputs, a full matrix has 331,776 entries. A rank-eight pair of matrices has 576 × 8 + 8 × 576 = 9,216 entries. This illustrative calculation explains why an adapter can contain fewer trainable parameters. It is not the complete parameter count of our model or all of its adapters.

“Frozen” means excluded from the optimizer's parameter updates. It does not mean the base model disappears, occupies no memory or stops participating in forward computation. The training calculation may still need activations through frozen layers to learn the adapter.

A self contained picture of generation and learning

flowchart TD
    P["Prompt tokens"] --> M["Model calculation"]
    W["Learned weights"] --> M
    M --> S["Predicted scores"]
    S --> C["Choose next token"]
    C --> D{"Continue generation?"}
    D -->|Yes: append token| P
    D -->|No| O["Completed output"]
    S --> L["Calculate training loss"]
    T["Correct training target"] --> L
    L --> G["Calculate gradients"]
    G --> U["Optimizer updates selected weights"]
    U --> W
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
    P["Prompt tokens"] --> M["Model calculation"]
    W["Learned weights"] --> M
    M --> S["Predicted scores"]
    S --> C["Choose next token"]
    C --> D{"Continue generation?"}
    D -->|Yes: append token| P
    D -->|No| O["Completed output"]
    S --> L["Calculate training loss"]
    T["Correct training target"] --> L
    L --> G["Calculate gradients"]
    G --> U["Optimizer updates selected weights"]
    U --> W

The generation loop uses the weights. The branch through a correct target, loss, gradients and optimizer is the training path. Ordinary inference does not take that branch.

families.title: Language model atlas
families.html:
Concept — A representative map of language modeling within machine learning. Implementation links state exactly which exercises run in this package.

Language models are machine learning

Concept — Field, task, and architecture are different labels. Machine learning means fitting a model from examples so it can make predictions or decisions on new inputs. A language model learns patterns that assign probabilities to language: for example, which token might come next or which token belongs in a missing position. A token is a processing unit such as a word, word fragment, or byte. Generating text is one use of those predictions.

Language models are part of machine learning. Many modern language models are deep neural networks. However, language modeling also includes count-based models that learn frequencies without a neural network. Deep learning is therefore not the parent of every language model. The Foundations and Language models tracks in this course belong to the same field.

flowchart TD
 M[Machine learning] --> C[Count-based estimation]
 M --> N[Neural networks]
 M --> O[Other learned models]
 C --> G[N-gram language models]
 N --> L[Neural language models]
 N --> V[Vision and other neural tasks]
 L --> D[Deep language models]
 O --> T[Trees and regression models]
Read the diagram algorithm
flowchart TD
 M[Machine learning] --> C[Count-based estimation]
 M --> N[Neural networks]
 M --> O[Other learned models]
 C --> G[N-gram language models]
 N --> L[Neural language models]
 N --> V[Vision and other neural tasks]
 L --> D[Deep language models]
 O --> T[Trees and regression models]

This is a representative relationship map, not a complete partition of machine learning. An n-gram is a sequence of n tokens; n is a number, not an acronym. All these learned language models are statistical in the broad sense. In this course, count-based identifies the non-neural baseline more precisely than treating “statistical” and “neural” as opposites. Deep learning uses multiple learned representation layers; not every neural network needs to be deep.

Natural language processing is the application area concerned with human language. A logistic regression spam classifier predicts a message label, so it is machine learning applied to language, but it is not itself a language model. An encoder pretrained to recover masked tokens has a language-modeling objective; after adaptation, its deployed output might instead be a document embedding or a category. A vector is an ordered list of numbers; an embedding is a learned vector representation. Neither an embedding output nor an encoder architecture alone proves language-model pretraining.

An algorithm for reading any model card

Instead of assigning one exclusive family, build a description by answering these questions:

DimensionQuestionExample answers
TaskWhat does it predict or generate?Next token, missing token, translation, image-conditioned answer
Learning signalWhere do training targets come from?Text itself, human labels, teacher outputs, preferences, environment rewards
Sequence mechanismHow does information move across positions?Counts, feed-forward window, convolution, recurrence, state space, attention, hybrid
Information flowWhich context can a prediction use?Earlier tokens, bidirectional context, encoded source plus generated prefix
Parameter routingWhich processing blocks run?Dense shared blocks or selected experts
Training historyWhat has already been learned?Pretrained base, instruction-tuned, domain-adapted, distilled
Modality and specialtyWhat inputs and domain does it support?Text, images and text, speech, code, mathematics
DeploymentHow is it stored and executed?Weight precision, total and active parameters, context budget, local or remote hardware

For example, one model can simultaneously be a neural, decoder-only, autoregressive, mixture-of-experts Transformer, instruction-tuned for code, with quantized weights. Autoregressive means predicting an output using earlier outputs. None of these labels replaces the others. Small and large describe scale, not separate mathematical architectures. A model's learned weights, data, training objective, and evaluation matter alongside its architecture.

Classify a real use case

Design activity: for an offline operations-note assistant, compare a count-based completion baseline, a tiny causal neural language model, and an adapted pretrained assistant. Record the eight dimensions above, which one you would build first, and one measurement that could change your choice. Use the statistical word-model lab, training from random weights lab, and adaptation lab for the implemented paths. The broader machine learning atlas shows the surrounding methods.

Explanation check: Is a quantized coding model a new architecture? No: coding is a specialty and quantization changes numerical representation. Is a count-based next-word predictor machine learning? Yes: its probabilities are estimated from examples, even though it does not use backpropagation. Is an instruction-tuned model pretrained? Yes: it already has trained parameters when you receive it.

Model families explained as algorithms

Runnable from-scratch paths now include causal Transformer, recurrent language model, masked encoder, encoder–decoder, and toy state-space, expert, and hybrid designs. The transfer comparison reuses a checkpoint you pretrain yourself. Diffusion remains Concept material.

Start with the count-based foundation, then read the picture top to bottom within each card. Its eight cards illustrate selected neural design choices, not an exhaustive family tree. A mixture of experts is often a component inside a Transformer. Encoder and decoder describe information-flow roles; they can also be built with Transformer layers. Recurrent and state space approaches overlap. Diffusion describes a modeling and generation framework that can use a Transformer as its denoising network.

Foundation: count-based language models

Concept, with a linked Runnable implementation lab. Use case: a small operations-note completion baseline that can run on a central processing unit. Historical speech recognition and text entry also used count-based language models; they are useful for learning probability before introducing neural networks. An order-two model estimates the next word from one preceding word. An order-three model uses two preceding words. Increasing the order increases context but also creates more rarely observed combinations.

Algorithm: split permitted text into training and evaluation sets; tokenize; count context–next-word combinations using only training text; smooth and normalize the counts; look up a new context; score or sample the next word. Repeating the last two steps generates a continuation. Training here estimates counts and probabilities rather than updating neural weights with gradients.

Worked example: after “server,” the training text has “starts” three times and “stops” once. Without smoothing their probabilities are 3/4 and 1/4. In a deliberately two-word output vocabulary, add-one smoothing gives (3+1)/(4+2) = 2/3 and (1+1)/(4+2) = 1/3. With more vocabulary options, the denominator must include every option, including an unknown-word symbol when used. Smoothing reserves probability for unobserved events.

Build from start to finish: open the statistical language-model lab. Define success as improving held-out probability assignment over its uniform baseline; use the included synthetic operations sentences; split before fitting vocabulary and counts; preserve the tokenizer and unknown-word policy; fit a smoothed counting model; choose context order using validation; save and reload the count tables and vocabulary; predict a new context through the local saved-model interface. The included teaching run evaluates validation performance, not production readiness. Before deployment, add an untouched external test set, audit memorized sensitive text, monitor unknown words and drift, and retain the previous artifact for rollback. Submit the report, probability plot, reload output, and one failed completion. This small exercise needs no Vast.ai rental. Its full build guide includes the input contract and deployment limitations.

Change one variable: compare context orders one and three on the same split. Explain why more context can worsen results with sparse data. Compare perplexity only when tokenization, vocabulary policy, and evaluation text are compatible. Perplexity summarizes how surprised a model is by the observed tokens; lower is better under those matched conditions.

Design 1 Dense decoder-only Transformer

Analogy: a writer can look back at earlier parts of the current passage, decide which are useful and then choose what to write next. The same editing process is applied at each layer. The mathematical attention process is not human awareness or deliberate reading.

The algorithm:

  1. Convert the available tokens into vectors and add information about their positions.
  2. At each layer, compute attention: score how useful allowed positions are to the current position.
  3. Convert those scores into weights and use them to combine information from the allowed positions.
  4. Apply a shared feed-forward transformation to each position. This transformation is a small neural network inside the larger model.
  5. Repeat these transformations through the layer stack.
  6. Convert the last position's final representation into vocabulary scores and choose a next token.
  7. Append the token and continue until a stopping rule is met.

Worked example: in “The red notebook belongs to Maya. Her notebook is ...”, earlier words can influence the next-token representation. We cannot infer from a convenient explanation that the model used one particular word unless we examine the actual computation. Attention scores are not a guaranteed causal explanation of an answer.

What dense means: the model normally uses the same shared processing blocks for each token rather than selecting a small subset of alternative expert blocks. It does not mean every stored scalar participates in every computation; an embedding lookup, for example, selects particular rows.

Technical detail: a causal mask prevents a position from attending to later positions. It is crucial during training because the correct next token must not be visible as context for its own prediction. With cached generation, earlier key and value vectors can be reused rather than recomputed from scratch. The cache occupies memory that grows with the retained context.

Try: run Lab 22, then inspect the causal-mask test in Lab 27. Change a future input token and check that earlier-position outputs remain unchanged.

Design 2 Mixture of experts

Analogy: a dispatcher sends a job to a small selection of available teams. All teams remain part of the organization, even when only some handle this job. The teams are learned mathematical networks; they need not correspond to human categories such as “math expert” or “history expert.”

The algorithm for one expert layer:

  1. Receive a token's current vector representation from the surrounding model.
  2. A router network assigns a score to each available expert.
  3. Select the highest-scoring one or few experts for that token.
  4. Send the token representation through the selected expert networks.
  5. Weight and combine their output vectors.
  6. Pass the result to the next part of the surrounding model.

Worked example: suppose four experts receive router probabilities 0.60, 0.25, 0.10 and 0.05. A top-two router selects the first two. A common design renormalizes their weights over the selected pair, producing approximately 0.706 and 0.294. A weighted combination of their vector outputs becomes the layer's output. Exact routing and normalization rules vary by architecture.

Why use it: more learned expert capacity can be available than is active for a single token. But all experts still require storage or offloading, and moving work between devices can introduce overhead.

Technical detail: routers can collapse toward a few experts. Many implementations introduce balancing losses, capacity constraints or specialized dispatch mechanisms. Top-k selection is discrete; training uses particular gating and gradient conventions. Our toy implementation deliberately omits many production features.

Try: run python mechanisms.py and count how many tokens reach each expert. Then change one router bias and observe whether routing becomes unbalanced.

Design 3 Recurrent neural network

Analogy: a reader keeps a short working note, updates it after every word, and uses that note when reading the next word. Information may be compressed or forgotten because the note has limited capacity.

The algorithm:

  1. Initialize an internal state, usually a vector of zeros or a learned starting state.
  2. Read the next token vector.
  3. Combine the token vector with the previous state using learned transformations.
  4. Apply nonlinear operations and, in gated variants, controls that regulate what to keep or overwrite.
  5. Use the new state to produce an output representation or prediction.
  6. Carry the new state into the next token's update.

Worked example: after reading “The delivery address changed to ...”, the state can carry information relevant to completing the address. It is a learned numerical representation, not a literal stored sentence. Details can disappear as more tokens update the state.

Technical detail: a basic recurrence can be written new_state = tanh(input_transform + previous_state_transform + bias). The hyperbolic tangent function limits its output to between -1 and 1. A gated recurrent unit adds learned controls to help manage state updates. Training usually propagates gradients through the sequence of state updates; very long chains create their own optimization challenges.

Try on paper: let a one-number state start at zero and update as new_state = 0.5 × old_state + current_input. Process inputs 2, 0 and 0. The states become 2, 1 and 0.5. This linear example illustrates memory decay; it is not a full recurrent neural network.

Design 4 State space model

Analogy: a compact internal system evolves as new observations arrive, a little like a simulated physical system with a current state. In a language model, the state is learned numerical memory rather than a literal description of a physical object.

A simplified discrete algorithm:

  1. Start with an internal state.
  2. Convert the current token representation into an input contribution.
  3. Transform the old state using a structured transition.
  4. Combine the transformed old state with the new input contribution.
  5. Read an output representation from the updated state.
  6. Carry the updated state forward and repeat.

One simplified mathematical form is state_t = A × state_previous + B × input_t, followed by output_t = C × state_t + D × input_t. Here A, B, C and D denote transformations; they are not acronyms. The actual dimensions and parameterization depend on the architecture.

Worked example: if A = 0.8, B = 1, the old state is 2 and the new scalar input is 3, the next state is 0.8 × 2 + 1 × 3 = 4.6. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a language model by itself.

What makes a selective state space model different: parts of the update depend on the current input. This allows the model to regulate which information affects the state. Mamba is a particular selective architecture with specialized design and implementation choices; our simple diagonal recurrence is not Mamba. [5]

Technical detail: a recurrent inference state can have fixed size as processed sequence length grows. Training may still store substantial activations, and a pure Python loop does not demonstrate the speed of an optimized parallel implementation. Compact state also creates a recall tradeoff: retaining a summary is not the same as retaining direct access to every earlier token.

Try: process a sequence all at once, then as two chunks while carrying the state between them. The included test checks that the outputs match for our toy recurrence.

Design 5 Hybrid model

Analogy: a worker keeps a compact running note but also consults parts of the original material when necessary. Different mechanisms address different parts of the task.

One illustrative algorithm:

  1. Convert the tokens into vector representations.
  2. Use a recurrent or state-based layer to summarize sequential information.
  3. Pass the resulting representations into an attention layer.
  4. Allow attention to use the context that this architecture makes available.
  5. Continue through the chosen mixture of layers and produce output scores.
  6. During generation, maintain whatever states and attention caches those layers need.

Worked example: our toy hybrid has a state space sequence-mixing layer and an attention sequence-mixing layer. This demonstrates that mechanisms can coexist. It does not establish that the combination outperforms either mechanism alone.

Technical detail: “hybrid” is a broad label. Full attention, local attention, recurrence and expert routing can be combined in different ways. A hybrid containing full attention can still have a growing attention cache. RecurrentGemma combines recurrence and local attention; it should not be described as a renamed Mamba model. [6]

Try: train the supplied toy Transformer, state space model and hybrid using the same number of updates. Then explain why differing parameter counts still prevent a fair architecture ranking.

Design 6 Encoder-only model

Analogy: an editor reads the whole sentence before deciding what it means or how to label it. The task is often understanding or representing the input rather than writing a long continuation.

The algorithm:

  1. Tokenize the complete input passage.
  2. Convert the token identifiers into vector representations.
  3. Mix information across the allowed input positions; bidirectional encoders can use both earlier and later context.
  4. Produce contextual representations for the input tokens.
  5. Use an appropriate output component to produce a class label, token labels or a representation for retrieval.

Worked example: “I deposited money at the bank” and “I sat beside the river bank” contain the same word, but surrounding words can change its representation. A classifier can then use that context to choose a category.

Technical detail: a pooled sentence representation can be used for similarity search when the model and training objective support that task. Arbitrarily averaging any encoder's hidden vectors does not guarantee high-quality retrieval embeddings. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers is one well-known encoder family. [15]

Try: define a three-class ticket classifier that returns a label directly. Compare this simpler output contract with a generator that must learn to produce correctly formatted text.

Design 7 Encoder–decoder model

Analogy: a reader first prepares a representation of a source document; a writer then produces an answer while consulting that representation and the answer written so far.

The algorithm:

  1. Tokenize the source text.
  2. Run the encoder over the source to produce contextual representations.
  3. Begin the output sequence with the appropriate starting marker.
  4. Let the decoder use earlier output tokens and the encoder's source representations.
  5. Predict the next output token.
  6. Append it and repeat until the output is complete.

Worked example: the source is “Translate to French: Good morning.” The decoder generates the translation while using the encoded source. The source and generated output are separate sequences.

Technical detail: in a Transformer encoder–decoder, decoder self-attention processes the output prefix; cross-attention uses representations produced by the encoder. Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer is a familiar family in this category. The five in its shortened name counts the five words beginning with T. [16]

Try: compare summarization with a decoder-only prompt and with an encoder–decoder model. Keep the source passages and evaluation criteria the same before comparing quality.

Design 8 Diffusion language modeling

Analogy: an editor fills blanks in a draft, revises uncertain parts and repeats. This differs from committing to one next token at every ordinary left-to-right step.

One masked-diffusion-style algorithm:

  1. Keep the conditioning prompt available.
  2. Initialize an output region containing mask symbols or another prescribed noisy representation.
  3. Predict possible tokens for multiple output positions.
  4. Choose which predictions to accept, keep masked or revise according to the model's sampling schedule.
  5. Repeat the refinement operation for several rounds.
  6. Stop according to the prescribed schedule or completion rule.

Worked example: a schematic output might move from [blank] [blank] [blank] to the [blank] sleeps and then the cat sleeps. Real subword tokenization, revision rules and training schedules differ from this word-level cartoon.

Technical detail: diffusion language models can operate in discrete token space or use other representations. Not every masked language model is a diffusion generator. Bidirectional training alone does not supply the iterative generation algorithm. Speed depends on the number of refinement rounds, implementation and task; predicting several positions at once does not guarantee lower latency.

For a discrete example, Large Language Diffusion with mAsking uses a forward masking process and a learned reverse generation process. Its denoising network is a Transformer. This demonstrates why “diffusion” and “Transformer” can describe the same model. Iterative masked generation is broader than diffusion: repeatedly filling blanks is not sufficient to establish that a model was trained with a diffusion formulation. [24]

Try on paper: describe what information is available in a left-to-right next-token prediction and in a masked-position prediction. Then explain why their training objectives and inference procedures need not be identical.

Additional sequence designs worth recognizing

Concept — Historical foundations and alternative sequence mechanisms. These entries broaden the map. The recurrent entry now has a runnable gated-recurrent-unit lab; standalone feed-forward-window, convolutional-language, and linear-attention implementations remain Concept project plans. Use the shared build plan below to turn each into a complete project. The existing convolution lesson classifies images and does not implement a convolutional language model.

DesignPlain algorithmReal-world use case and tradeoff
Feed-forward neural language modelEmbed a fixed window of previous words; concatenate the vectors; apply a neural network; predict the next wordCompact short-context completion or a research baseline; cannot see beyond its selected window [22]
Causal convolutional language modelSlide learned filters over earlier token representations; stack gated layers; predict the next tokenText completion with parallel training over positions; finite receptive field limits accessible context [23]
Gated recurrent language modelUpdate a running state using gates that control retention and replacement; predict from the stateStreaming text prediction; long short-term memory networks and gated recurrent units are variants, not separate learning paradigms

For the fixed-window network, change the window from two to four words; for a convolution, calculate the receptive field; for recurrence, explain what must fit in the state; for linear attention, identify the accumulated state in the chosen formulation. Explain how each prevents future-token leakage. Use the additional build plans for encoder, recurrent, encoder–decoder, and diffusion project assessments.

Architecture, objective, and generation are not interchangeable

Training objectiveTraining targetTypical examples and boundary
Causal next-token predictionNext token from the allowed prefixCount-based, recurrent, convolutional, state-space, and decoder-only Transformer models can all support this
Masked-token predictionHidden token from visible contextUsed in Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers pretraining; a fill-mask objective alone does not supply a chat-generation procedure
Sequence-to-sequence predictionTarget output conditioned on a sourceTranslation or summarization; often an encoder–decoder, but conditional generation also works with decoder-only models
Denoising or diffusion objectiveRecover information from a specified corruption processA diffusion formulation specifies the corruption, training objective, and reverse process; not every denoising model is a diffusion model

Teaching boundary: an embedding model, reranker, reasoning-tuned model, coding model, vision-language model, and on-device model need not define six new architectures. Describe their task, modality, training history, and deployment separately. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies retrieved context to a generation system; it is a system pattern, not a new neural architecture.

How specialization changes the algorithm

The core architecture does not have to change every time the task changes. Training data, training objective, input representation and output checks can produce different specializations.

The table below mixes tasks, modalities, and a deployment choice for practical comparison. The on-device row is a deployment target, not a specialization or separate model family.

SpecializationThe practical algorithmWhat to measure
CodingRead a specification and relevant code; generate a proposed program; execute approved tests in an isolated runner; record failuresTests passed, correctness on unseen tasks, runtime and unsupported operations
Reasoning or mathematicsRead a problem; generate an answer or intermediate work; check the final result using suitable rules or independent evidenceCorrect final answers and robust behavior under rewording; explanation length is not the score
Vision and languageConvert image pixels into features; connect them to text representations; generate text conditioned on bothGrounded answers to questions about the image, including negative and ambiguous cases
Audio and languageConvert audio into an appropriate representation; combine it with the language system; produce text or another supported outputTranscription or task correctness, timing and performance under noise
Domain adaptationCollect representative domain examples; train or retrieve as appropriate; evaluate on separately sourced examplesDomain accuracy and whether general capabilities regress
On-device deploymentSelect a task-suitable model; fit it into the device budget; use supported computation kernels; measure quality and responsivenessTotal memory, latency, energy where measurable and offline operation

A trained language model alone is not an agent. An agent application adds a control loop, available tools, state and rules for taking actions. A model that writes a shell command has not necessarily executed it. That distinction matters when evaluating a future coding system.

Reference map of the model design choices

A small language model is a language model small enough for some constrained use case. There is no universal parameter cutoff. The approximate 100 million to 10 billion range is a useful teaching convention, not an industry standard. A model with 500 million parameters can still exceed a particular phone's memory budget, while a workstation can run much larger models.

Describe a model along several separate axes. For example: “a dense Transformer with 135 million parameters, pretrained for next-token prediction, instruction-tuned for text, deployed using 32-bit floating-point precision on a central processing unit.” These labels describe different properties of the same model.

Architecture describes the computation

The table combines frequently encountered designs for comparison. Read the dimension table above first: routing, information flow, sequence mechanism, and generation framework can overlap within one model. Count-based and additional neural designs are covered in the preceding algorithm sections.

Design choicePlain-language pictureTechnical ideaWhy use itMain difficulty
Dense decoder-only TransformerEvery token passes through the same stack of processing layersCausal attention mixes previous-token information; feed-forward layers transform each positionText generation, chat, code, small agentsAttention and cached context consume memory and compute
Sparse mixture of expertsA router chooses a few processing teams for each tokenSelected expert feed-forward networks execute instead of one shared dense blockMore total capacity at a given amount of active computationAll experts still need storage; routing and communication add overhead
Recurrent modelA reader updates a running summary after each tokenHidden state is updated sequentially, as in a recurrent neural network or gated recurrent unitStreaming and compact demonstrationsCompression into a state can lose details; training and hardware tradeoffs
State space modelA structured memory evolves as the sequence arrivesA state transition summarizes prior inputs; selective state space models make parts of the transition input-dependentLong streams and compact inference stateOptimized kernels and precise recall can be challenging
HybridSome layers keep a compact state; others use attentionCombines mechanisms such as recurrence, local attention or full attentionBalance recall, speed and memoryBehavior depends on the exact mixture; memory is not automatically constant
Encoder-only modelRead the entire passage before representing itBidirectional context, often trained with masked-token objectivesClassification, embeddings, search and rerankingUsually not an autoregressive chat generator
Encoder–decoder modelRead an input, then produce an outputAn encoder represents the input; a decoder generates using that representationTranslation, summarization and other text-to-text tasksTwo interacting components and a different training interface

This course starts its pretrained generation track with a dense Transformer because the included tooling and exercises support it. Examples include SmolLM2, small Llama, Gemma and Qwen checkpoints. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers family models illustrate encoder-only approaches; Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer family models illustrate encoder–decoder approaches. The count-based lab is an even simpler starting point for understanding language modeling itself. The architecture alone does not determine quality.

Mixture of experts correction: active parameter count is not total parameter count. Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B has about 14.3 billion total parameters and 2.7 billion active parameters. DeepSeek-V2-Lite has about 16 billion total and 2.4 billion active. These are useful mixture of experts examples, but they are not tiny memory-footprint models. Do not budget their weight memory as if they contained only the active parameters. [3, 4]

Attention correction: ordinary full attention compares token positions in pairs, giving quadratic attention computation with sequence length. Naively storing attention scores is also quadratic, but memory-efficient implementations can avoid materializing that full matrix. During autoregressive inference, a standard Transformer key–value cache grows approximately linearly with context length. A state space model's recurrent state can remain fixed-size with respect to processed length during inference; this does not mean its training memory, input storage or total runtime is constant. [5]

RecurrentGemma uses the Griffin hybrid design, including recurrence and local attention. It should not simply be described as a Mamba model. Hybrid architectures can have very different state and cache behavior. [6]

Training stage describes how the model learned to behave

LabelWhat happenedWhat it means in practice
PretrainedParameters were already learned before your present use or adaptationDescribes training history; both a base checkpoint and an instruction-tuned checkpoint can be pretrained
BaseIn this language-model context, a checkpoint before instruction or preference post-trainingOften optimized for a pretraining objective such as next-token prediction; not automatically an assistant
Instruction-tunedTrained on requests and desired responsesBetter suited to an assistant-style interface
Domain-adaptedContinued pretraining or supervised tuning on a domainMay improve on domain tasks; requires domain-specific evaluation
Preference-tunedLearned from preferred versus less preferred outputs or other feedbackCan improve selected behaviors without guaranteeing correctness
Reasoning-orientedTrained to perform better on multi-step tasks, often with additional post-trainingEvaluate answer correctness, cost and robustness; a long explanation is not proof of reasoning
DistilledLearned from a teacher's outputs, distributions or intermediate representationsOften transfers useful behavior into a smaller student

Fine-tuning and pretraining change parameters. Prompting and ordinary retrieval-augmented generation do not. A conversation is not automatically a training run.

These labels are not exclusive. A model may be pretrained, domain-adapted, instruction-tuned, and distilled. Pretraining can use self-supervised targets derived from data, supervised targets, or combinations; it does not always mean next-token prediction or require an internet-scale corpus. Our tiny from-scratch lab learns on a small corpus and has correspondingly limited capability.

A vision-language model generally needs an image processor, a vision representation and a way to connect it to the language model. Adding image bytes to a text prompt does not create vision capability.

The named .gguf format is a model file format that can contain various precisions and quantization types. Activation-aware weight quantization is a quantization approach; ExLlama version 2 quantized format is a quantized representation and associated tooling. They are not interchangeable names for the same mathematical operation. The glossary explains the exact format identifiers without inventing expansions for proper names. Neither mixture of experts nor speculative decoding guarantees a particular speedup on your hardware. [9, 10, 11, 13]
