Elo is a comparative rating system named after its inventor, not an acronym. For equal ratings, the expected score is 0.5. With an update factor of 16, one win adds eight points to the winner and subtracts eight from the loser. The exercise updates two ratings from valid judge choices. Wrong judgments can produce a confidently misleading ranking. Ratings depend on opponents, presentation order, update rules and the population of comparisons.

Case banks: validation and test contain six different authored questions each. The selected bank appears in both answer orders, producing twelve presentations of six cases. IDs and questions are saved with the raw judgments; swapped orders are not independent new examples.

Build from start to finish: run fixture mode first, then actual-model mode. Inspect judge-audit.png, raw outputs, invalid responses, agreement and Elo. This lab freezes the judge and saves evaluation artifacts rather than training a new checkpoint. For a product, add blinded human review on representative examples and measure disagreement before using a judge to gate releases.

Assessment: explain why the biased fixture can be valid and consistent but wrong; identify a malformed actual judge output; propose controls for order, length and self-preference bias. Monitoring: version the judge, rubric and prompt; retest when any changes; retain a manual review route and previous scoring configuration.

streaming-service | Serve a model and measure when tokens arrive

Tag: Runnable implementation lab. Scope: real local HTTP streaming, measured from a client. HTTP means Hypertext Transfer Protocol. This is a single-process teaching service, not a production endpoint.

Two phases matter: prefill processes the prompt; decode generates subsequent tokens. A key-value cache avoids repeating some earlier computation. A longer prompt can increase prefill work even when output length is unchanged. Optimized batching and kernels can change performance; the Python reference implementation measures only its own behavior.

Time to first token is elapsed time from request start to the first observed token. Time per output token here means (last_token_time - first_token_time) / (output_tokens - 1). A one-token response has no subsequent-token interval, so the value is absent rather than zero. Inter-token latency is the gap between successive observed tokens. The report includes its 95th percentile. Whole-request duration includes overhead after the last token as well.

Worked example: first token at 0.20 seconds, last token at 0.50 seconds, and four output tokens gives 0.10 seconds per subsequent token. Dividing 0.50 by four instead gives a different quantity, 0.125 seconds per token including initial wait. Always name the measurement boundary.

    C["Local client starts timer"] --> H["Loopback HTTP service"]
    H --> P["Prompt prefill"]
    P --> F["First token arrives"]
    P --> K["Key-value cache"]
    K --> D["Decode next token"]
    D --> S["Stream token to client"]
    S --> D
    S --> M["Arrival timestamps and latency report"]
    F --> M
Read the diagram algorithm

    H --> P["Prompt prefill"]

Evidence boundary: this is a fixed local systems-timing probe. Its twelve requests do not form a validation/test quality split, and --split is not applicable. The data card names training data separately from the two timing prompts.

Build from start to finish: the serving experiment trains and saves a small grouped-query model, reload-checks it, starts a private loopback service, sends real streaming requests, and shuts the service down. It tests two prompt lengths with cached and uncached generation and three repeats per condition. Inspect the actual arrival curves in latency.png. The service sends token identifiers as newline-delimited JavaScript Object Notation; the client timestamps each line.

For manual use, run python modern_serving.py --model-dir outputs/your-serving-run from the lab/ directory using your environment's Python. It prints a temporary local request token and binds port 8766. The website remains on 8765. Keep the token local and stop the process with Control+C. The source contains request_tokens for a sample client.

Assessment: calculate the numerical example, explain warm versus cold starts, compare cached outputs, and report variation without claiming a universal speedup. Operating-system scheduling and HTTP buffering can affect observations. This experiment does not test concurrent users or internet transport.

Deployment and monitoring: measure peak memory, p50/p95 latency across enough requests, throughput at stated concurrency, timeouts and quality under load. Add authentication, resource limits, logging, isolation and a deployment review before exposing any service beyond your machine. Retain the previous model and serving configuration for rollback.

modern-capstone | Defend the complete engineering decision

Tag: Concept. Assessment project using the tested implementations above. Do not mark complete solely because a process exited successfully.

Choose one product: an offline operations-note completer, a ticket-routing assistant, or a verifier-backed arithmetic demonstrator. Write the intended user, input contract, output contract, success criterion, unacceptable errors and resource limits. The arithmetic demonstration is educational; it does not replace a deterministic calculator.

Build from start to finish: gather permitted data or explicitly label synthetic data; preserve document/template/group splits; implement a baseline; choose a model and tokenizer; train from scratch or adapt a checkpoint; record the complete training cost; compare one architecture or training change; freeze settings; run the independent test once; inspect failures; save weights, configuration and data identity; reload and predict new inputs; serve locally; measure latency and memory; write monitoring and rollback instructions.

Required evidence: model and data cards; source version; environment; seeds; exact commands; training/validation/test split IDs; raw predictions; saved/reloaded equivalence; quality and uncertainty; memory accounting; timing boundaries; known failed examples; and a reproduction procedure. Include three concise research annotations: the problem each paper addressed, the idea you used, and the part you did not reproduce.

Compare honestly: a model with more experts has more stored capacity; a quantized selected projection does not make the whole model four-bit; pass at four spends more generation than one attempt; a learned judge can be biased; and a verifier can reward a loophole. An improvement in one measurement can trade away another.

Assessment rubric: an engineer should be able to reproduce your result, identify the evidence boundary, inspect one failed example, and explain the next data or system investment. Production readiness requires representative real data, broader reliability and security assessment, and operational ownership beyond this classroom capstone. Keep the foundational machine-learning and retrieval paths available; a language model is one possible component, not the default solution to every problem.

research-landmarks.title: Landmark research: ideas and evidence
research-landmarks.html:
Landmark research: ideas, evidence, and the path to today's models

Explore The Transformer turning point for a 3D architecture, a numerical attention activity, and the history behind the 2017 paper.

Tag: Concept and research-reading workshop. This is a selected learning history, not a claim that these papers were the first or only contributions to each idea. Dates usually refer to the first public paper or preprint; conference and journal dates can differ. Research is cumulative and branching, not one uninterrupted product lineage.

For each source, read in this order: the problem; the main figure; one worked algorithm; the experimental setup; the limitations. Then connect it to an executable lesson. A teaching mechanism is not a reproduction of the paper's scale, dataset or results. The page links primary papers and official benchmark documentation; some publishers can require access or block automated fetching.

Foundations that make learning possible

Year and primary sourceContribution to understandSuper Lab connection and boundary
1986 — Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Learning representations by back-propagating errorsPropagate error derivatives through multilayer networks to learn internal representations. Backpropagation has earlier mathematical and computational antecedents.Deep learning: trace a gradient and train a nonlinear classifier. Automatic differentiation implements the calculation; it does not choose a good dataset.
1997 — Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, Long Short-Term MemoryGated recurrent memory addresses learning over extended sequences.Recurrent language model: compare state and context. The included simple recurrent build is not a long short-term memory implementation.
2001 — Breiman, Random ForestsCombine randomized trees to improve prediction and reduce instability.Ensembles: compare one tree, forests and boosting. Language models are one part of machine learning, not a replacement for tabular baselines.
2003 — Bengio and colleagues, A Neural Probabilistic Language ModelLearn distributed word representations jointly with a probabilistic language model.Language model atlas and count-based baseline: contrast counts with learned representations. A useful precursor to embeddings and neural language prediction.
2013/2014 — Kingma and Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational BayesLearn latent-variable generative models with a tractable variational objective and reparameterized gradients.Variational autoencoder: inspect reconstruction and divergence tradeoffs. Its divergence term is not a direct accuracy metric.
2014 — Goodfellow and colleagues, Generative Adversarial NetworksTrain a generator against a discriminator through an adversarial objective.Adversarial generation: inspect samples and coverage. Low training loss alone does not establish high-quality generation.
2014/2015 — Kingma and Ba, Adam: A Method for Stochastic OptimizationUse moving estimates of gradient moments to adapt parameter updates.Deep learning and model builds. The course often uses AdamW, whose decoupled weight decay is a later modification, not simply an alternative spelling of Adam.

From sequence models to reusable Transformer representations

Year and primary sourceContribution to understandSuper Lab connection and boundary
2014/2015 — Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and TranslateLearn which source representations to consult while producing a translation. Attention existed before the Transformer.Encoder–decoder build: follow source information into decoder predictions.
2015/2016 — He and colleagues, Deep Residual Learning for Image RecognitionLearn residual transformations around identity paths to support deep optimization.Block components: distinguish adding a residual from attending over earlier depth.
2015 — Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural NetworkTransfer information from teacher output distributions to a student.Distillation: calculate softened distributions and student gradients. The local demonstration is not a full teacher/student production pipeline.
2016 — Ba, Kiros and Hinton, Layer NormalizationNormalize a layer's activations within an example, with learned rescaling.Block components: compare normalization placements and root mean square scaling.
2017 — Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You NeedBuild an encoder–decoder sequence model from attention and position-wise transformations.Attention and cache, scratch model, and encoder–decoder. Modern decoder-only models modify this design; the original diagram is not universal.
2017 — Shazeer and colleagues, Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts LayerRoute inputs through selected expert networks to separate total capacity from per-example computation.Expert routing: inspect load balance and total storage. The local top-one router omits distributed capacity handling.
2018 — Devlin and colleagues, BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language UnderstandingPretrain bidirectional representations with a masked-language objective and adapt them to tasks.Masked encoder: hide targets and use surrounding context. The tiny build is not a reproduction of the complete original training recipe.
2019/2020 — Raffel and colleagues, Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text TransformerStudy transfer learning through a common text-to-text framework and denoising pretraining.Pretrained versus scratch and transfer comparison. Reuse and fine-tuning need task-specific evaluation.

Across modalities and domains

These papers connect the first Stanford slide's shared Transformer idea to concrete input representations. They are Concept reading bridges; the course's smaller existing builds have different architectures and training budgets.

ResearchContributionConnection to the lab
2020/2021 — Dosovitskiy and colleagues, An Image is Worth 16x16 WordsProcess image patches as a sequence for image recognition.Vision and language: identify the visual representation and its interface to text. The included pretrained vision lesson is not a reproduction of this paper.
2021 — Chen and colleagues, Decision TransformerCondition sequence modeling of actions on desired returns and past trajectory information.Reinforcement learning: contrast offline conditional sequence learning with value updates and policy gradients.
2021 — Ying and colleagues, Do Transformers Really Perform Bad for Graph Representation?Encode graph structure in the Graphormer Transformer.Graph neural networks: compare structural attention biases with neighborhood aggregation; the included graph build uses the latter.
2022 — Radford and colleagues, Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak SupervisionTrain Whisper using broad multilingual speech supervision.Engineering map: define audio preprocessing, target tokens, and evaluation. A speech-training implementation is not included.

Architecture and inference efficiency

Year and primary sourceContribution to understandSuper Lab connection and boundary
2019 — Shazeer, Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You NeedShare keys and values across query heads to reduce inference memory bandwidth requirements.Attention and cache: measure multi-query storage against multi-head storage.
2019 — Zhang and Sennrich, Root Mean Square Layer NormalizationNormalize using root mean square without the mean-centering step.Block components: compute the numeric normalization and compare trained models.
2020 — Shazeer, GLU Variants Improve TransformerStudy gated linear unit variants, including Swish-gated feed-forward layers.Block components: compare the gated and ordinary branches while disclosing parameter budgets.
2020 — Henry and colleagues, Query-Key Normalization for TransformersNormalize queries and keys and learn attention scaling to address score saturation.Block components: our root-mean-square variant illustrates normalization, but differs from the paper's Euclidean normalization and learned scaling.
2021 — Su and colleagues, RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position EmbeddingUse rotations to encode position and relative relationships in attention.Block components: inspect coordinate rotations and cache correctness.
2021/2022 — Press, Smith and Lewis, Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length ExtrapolationAdd distance-dependent attention biases and study length extrapolation.Block components: the course does not claim arbitrary-length generalization from a small fixed-context test.
2022 — Dao and colleagues, FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-AwarenessReorganize exact attention computation to reduce memory traffic and avoid storing the full score matrix. IO means input/output.Streaming and serving: distinguish an algorithm's mathematical result from an efficient kernel. The Python attention code is not FlashAttention.
2023 — Ainslie and colleagues, GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head CheckpointsGroup query heads over a smaller number of key/value heads and study conversion from multi-head models.Attention and cache: the lab trains variants from scratch; it does not implement the paper's uptraining procedure.
2023 — Jiang and colleagues, Mistral 7BCombine efficient attention choices, including grouped queries and sliding windows, in a capable language model.Attention and cache: study a window mask without claiming to reproduce Mistral's model or runtime.
2023 — Kwon and colleagues, Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttentionManage key/value cache allocations in blocks to improve serving utilization.Streaming and serving: distinguish cache representation from memory allocation. No paged allocator is implemented in this course.
2023 — Gu and Dao, Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State SpacesUse input-dependent selective state-space mechanisms for sequence modeling.Other families: the existing diagonal recurrence teaches state, not Mamba's full selective architecture.
2024 — DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language ModelCombine multi-head latent attention with an expert architecture to reduce resource costs.Latent caches: our compressed cache omits projection absorption, decoupled rotary handling and other model details.
2026 — Kimi Team and colleagues, Attention ResidualsReplace uniform depth accumulation with learned attention over earlier representations; study a block variant.Depth mechanisms: our block-output mixture is illustrative, not the full method or its memory/communication implementation.

Adaptation, retrieval, preferences, and rewards

Year and primary sourceContribution to understandSuper Lab connection and boundary
2017 — Schulman and colleagues, Proximal Policy Optimization AlgorithmsOptimize policies using surrogate objectives that constrain changes relative to sampled old-policy behavior.Policy optimization: the local terminal-return example has a limited critic and omits generalized advantage estimation.
2020 — Lewis and colleagues, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP TasksCombine retrieved non-parametric evidence with neural generation. NLP means natural language processing.Retrieval workshop: the lexical teaching retriever is not the paper's jointly trained retrieval setup. Ordinary retrieval need not update the generator.
2021 — Hu and colleagues, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language ModelsLearn low-rank parameter updates while freezing the underlying model.Adaptation comparison: inspect rank, parameter counts, frozen weights and saved adapter identity.
2022 — Ouyang and colleagues, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedbackCombine demonstrations, preference-based reward modeling and policy optimization to improve instruction following.Preference learning, reward model, and policy updates. Our synthetic examples are not human-feedback data collection.
2023 — Dettmers and colleagues, QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMsAdapt a frozen quantized model with NormalFloat4, double quantization and memory-management techniques. LLM means large language model.Optional cloud extension: the local uniform packed-weight demo is intentionally distinct, and the cloud extension uses ordinary AdamW.
2023 — Rafailov and colleagues, Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward ModelOptimize a preference objective directly from response comparisons relative to a reference policy.Preference learning: standard offline direct preference optimization avoids a separate reward-model training and online rollout loop.
2024 — Shao and colleagues, DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language ModelsIntroduce group relative policy optimization in a mathematical-language-model training study.Policy optimization: inspect group reward normalization and zero-variance groups.
2025 — DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement LearningStudy reward-driven reasoning behavior, including a reinforcement-learning-first model and a multi-stage pipeline.Verifier-backed token policy: the course uses a supervised warm start and constrained two-digit answers, not open-ended reasoning reproduction.
2025 — Zheng and colleagues, Group Sequence Policy OptimizationUse sequence-level importance ratios and clipping for language-model reinforcement learning.Policy optimization: calculate the length-normalized ratio; do not replace it with an unnormalized likelihood product.

Evaluation landmarks and official benchmark homes

Year and primary sourceContribution to understandSuper Lab connection and boundary
2020/2021 — Hendrycks and colleagues, Measuring Massive Multitask Language UnderstandingEvaluate broad subject knowledge and problem-solving across many tasks.Benchmark literacy: freeze dataset and prompting protocol, rather than reporting a homemade quiz as this benchmark.
2023 — Zheng and colleagues, Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot ArenaStudy language-model judging, human preference comparisons and judge biases.Judge audit: test strict output validity, order swaps, length bias and reference agreement.
2023 — Jimenez and colleagues, SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?Evaluate code changes against real repository issues and tests.Benchmark literacy: tools, repository environments and tests are part of the evaluation system. Official benchmark variants.
2023 — Rein and colleagues, GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A BenchmarkCreate expert-written science questions designed to be difficult even with ordinary information lookup. Q&A means question and answer.Benchmark literacy: domain difficulty and product relevance are separate considerations.
2025 — Phan and colleagues, Humanity's Last ExamCollect challenging academic questions to measure frontier capabilities.Benchmark literacy: track exact dataset versions and protocol. Official project.
Ongoing — Mathematical Association of America, American Invitational Mathematics ExaminationA mathematics competition, not originally a language-model training method.Evaluation harness: original arithmetic exercises are not examination questions or official scores; record exam year and protocol for any real benchmark use.

    S --> A["Attention and Transformers"]
    A --> E["Efficient components and caches"]
    A --> T["Reuse and adapt learned weights"]

Arrows connect engineering questions for this course, not exclusive historical ancestry. For example, recurrent models, convolutional models, statistical methods and state-space models remain useful; research did not simply replace every earlier family with Transformers.

Read a paper as an engineer

  1. State the specific problem and baseline the authors investigated.
  2. Expand each acronym and draw the information flow in your own words.
  3. Work through a two-token or two-parameter numerical example.
  4. List assumptions, dataset versions, training budget and evaluation protocol.
  5. Identify one claim the experiment supports and one broader claim it does not.
  6. Run the related Super Lab mechanism, then record differences from the original paper.
  7. Propose one controlled follow-up experiment and estimate its resource cost before running it.

Assessment artifact: a one-page research card containing title, authors, year/version, primary URL, problem, algorithm, evidence, limitations, related lesson, and your measured reproduction scope. Do not copy an abstract as your explanation. Do not describe a tiny synthetic exercise as reproducing a frontier model's capability.

Reading order for this expansion: attention and Transformer; multi-query and grouped-query attention; normalization and rotary positions; low-rank adaptation; direct preference optimization; policy optimization and group methods; judging and serving. Return to the foundational papers when the math or learning assumptions are unclear.

modern-glossary.title: Modern language-model terminology
modern-glossary.html:
Modern language-model terminology

Labels below answer different questions. A single model can be a decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, pretrained on next-token prediction, adapted with low-rank matrices, and deployed inside a retrieval system.

TermExpanded nameMeaning and learning destination
MHAMulti-head attentionSeveral query/key/value attention heads; cache build
MQAMulti-query attentionSeveral query heads share one key/value head; cache build
GQAGrouped-query attentionGroups of query heads share key/value heads; cache build
MLAMulti-head latent attentionCompressed latent key/value representation; research mechanisms
SWASliding-window attentionA position directly attends within a limited local window; cache build
AttnResAttention ResidualsLearned attention across earlier layer representations; research mechanisms
MoEMixture of expertsA router selects expert computations; expert costs
RoPERotary position embeddingPosition-dependent rotations of query/key coordinates; block components
ALiBiAttention with linear biasesDistance-proportional attention-score biases; block components
LNLayer normalizationPer-token feature normalization with learned scale and shift; block components
RMSNormRoot mean square normalizationScale by root mean square without mean subtraction; block components
QKNormQuery-key normalizationA family of attention query/key normalization choices; paper variants differ; block components
SwiGLUSwish-gated linear unitA feed-forward transformation with a Swish-controlled multiplicative gate; block components
SiLUSigmoid linear unitActivation x × sigmoid(x), also called Swish
GELUGaussian error linear unitSmooth activation used by the baseline feed-forward network
SFTSupervised fine-tuningLearn desired responses from examples; tuning comparison
PEFTParameter-efficient fine-tuningAdapt a relatively small parameter subset; also a software-library name
LoRALow-rank adaptationTrain small factorized updates to frozen matrices; tuning comparison
QLoRAQuantized low-rank adaptationAdapt a quantized frozen base; the paper uses NormalFloat4, double quantization and paged optimizers; cloud extension
NF4Four-bit NormalFloatA nonuniform four-bit representation motivated by normally distributed weights
DPODirect preference optimizationTrain using preferred/rejected responses relative to a reference policy; preference build
RLReinforcement learningLearn a policy using rewards from actions and outcomes
RLHFReinforcement learning from human feedbackHuman feedback guides reward-based policy optimization
RLVRReinforcement learning with verifiable rewardsA programmatically checkable outcome supplies reward; token policy
RMReward modelA learned scoring model; reward build
PPOProximal policy optimizationA policy optimization family using constrained/clipped update objectives; policy comparison
GRPOGroup relative policy optimizationUses response-group reward comparisons and policy ratios; policy comparison
GSPOGroup sequence policy optimizationUses sequence-level importance ratios and clipping; policy comparison
AIMEAmerican Invitational Mathematics ExaminationMathematics competition whose questions can be used under a specified evaluation protocol
HLEHumanity's Last ExamA named difficult academic question benchmark; versions matter
MMLUMassive Multitask Language UnderstandingA named broad subject evaluation
SWE-benchSoftware-engineering benchmarkRepository issue-resolution evaluation; variants and agent harness matter
GPQAGraduate-Level Google-Proof Question AnsweringExpert-written science-question evaluation
PPLPerplexityExponential of average negative log probability under the stated tokenization
LaaJLarge language model as a judgeUse a language model to assess outputs against a rubric; judge audit
KLKullback–Leibler divergenceDirectional distribution difference; not symmetric and not an accuracy score
Pass@kPass at kAt least one correct candidate among k attempts under the sampling protocol
EloNamed after Arpad Elo; not an acronymComparative ratings updated from outcomes
TTFTTime to first tokenDelay from request start to first observed token
TPOTTime per output tokenHere: average subsequent-token interval, excluding initial wait
ITLInter-token latencyObserved gap between successive tokens
KV cacheKey-value cacheTemporary attention state retained during generation
CPUCentral processing unitGeneral-purpose processor used for the core teaching experiments
GPUGraphics processing unitParallel processor useful for larger tensor workloads
VRAMVideo random-access memoryCommon name for graphics-device memory; total needs exceed stored weight bytes
CUDACompute Unified Device ArchitectureNVIDIA's graphics-processor computing platform
HTTPHypertext Transfer ProtocolRequest/response protocol used by the local streaming service
JSONJavaScript Object NotationStructured report and request format
SSHSecure ShellEncrypted remote connection and port-forwarding protocol
SCPSecure copyFile-copy command commonly used over Secure Shell

Read a metric before comparing it: record the denominator, tokenizer, dataset version, model revision, prompt, tools, sampling settings, time boundary, and hardware. A percentage without a protocol is not enough evidence for an engineering decision.

Classify this example: supervised fine-tuning using low-rank adaptation on a grouped-query Transformer, with retrieval at inference and a judged evaluation. The five labels respectively describe a training objective, parameter updates, architecture, evidence access, and evaluation. None replaces the others.

qlora-cloud.title: Quantized adaptation and cloud costs
qlora-cloud.html:
Quantized adaptation and a bounded cloud experiment

Tag: Concept / optional hardware-specific extension. All core modern-track experiments run on a central processing unit. lab/qlora_gpu.py contains a genuine NormalFloat4 loading/adaptation path, but its graphics-processor execution was not tested in the CPU release environment. Do not interpret source compilation or dependency installation as proof of a completed graphics-processor run.

The local packed4 branch is intentionally different: it uses uniform quantization on selected projections, packs two codes into each byte, and unpacks to floating point for computation. The optional extension uses a compatible bitsandbytes backend, a four-bit NormalFloat quantizer, double quantization of constants, and trainable low-rank adapters. It uses ordinary AdamW rather than a paged optimizer, so it does not claim to reproduce every QLoRA paper mechanism.

Decide before renting

  1. Finish the local baseline. Record model size, sequence length, batch size, training time and memory.
  2. Decide whether the goal requires this backend or a larger experiment. A cloud instance is not necessary simply to understand quantization.
  3. Choose a hardware/runtime combination supported by the current bitsandbytes installation guidance and quantized adaptation guidance.
  4. Compare live offers in Vast.ai. Price, availability, reliability, disk allocation and transfer charges vary. This guide supplies no invented hourly quote.
  5. Set an affordable maximum runtime and spending budget. A long-context or multi-model reinforcement-learning job needs a different estimate than this tiny adapter exercise.
Budget componentCalculation or check
ComputeObserved hourly rate × planned hours, including setup and idle time
StorageAllocated space × retained duration × applicable storage rate
TransferApplicable ingress/egress charges from the selected offer
HeadroomFailed runs, downloads, checkpoint saves and startup overhead
MemoryBase tensors + quantization metadata + adapters + gradients + optimizer + activations + temporary buffers

Worked cost exercise: if your chosen offer shows rate R and you plan two hours, compute cost is 2R. Add the actual storage and transfer terms. R is a learner-entered rate, not a quoted market price. Write down what you will do if the first measured run takes twice the expected time.

Connect from Windows, macOS, or Linux

Use Vast.ai's current connection instructions and the host/port shown for your own instance. Prefer a maintained PyTorch template with the intended CUDA support already installed. Inspect the template and provider controls before placing data on it. Use original public teaching data for this exercise.

From Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt, use the built-in OpenSSH client if installed. Replace the example host and port with the values Vast.ai provides; do not type the placeholders literally.

text
ssh -p 12345 root@YOUR_INSTANCE_HOST

The same command works from a macOS or Linux terminal. root must match the account provided by the selected template. No Git Bash is required on Windows.

Remote Linux shell only:

bash
nvidia-smi
python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__); print(torch.cuda.is_available()); print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'No CUDA device')"
git clone https://github.com/zelicerica/machine-learning-super-lab.git
cd machine-learning-super-lab
python -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-cloud
.venv-cloud/bin/python -m pip install -r lab/requirements.txt -r lab/requirements-foundations.txt
.venv-cloud/bin/python -m pip install bitsandbytes
.venv-cloud/bin/python -m pip check
.venv-cloud/bin/python -m pip freeze > cloud-environment.txt

This isolated environment can reuse the template's graphics-enabled PyTorch; inspect pip check and the versions before training. Do not install the laptop's processor-only PyTorch wheel over the cloud image. The bitsandbytes version is intentionally selected against current hardware support, then recorded in the environment file; this is not a pinned universally compatible cloud environment.

bash
cd lab
../.venv-cloud/bin/python lab.py doctor
../.venv-cloud/bin/python lab.py lock
../.venv-cloud/bin/python qlora_gpu.py --steps 5 --output outputs/nf4-smoke-01
../.venv-cloud/bin/python qlora_gpu.py --steps 30 --output outputs/nf4-train-01

Five updates check the workflow. Thirty do not establish model quality. Inspect finite losses, validation behavior, actual memory and the saved/reloaded logit comparison. The adapter must be reloaded against the same pinned base revision. Use the existing ticket benchmark only as a teaching check; broader independent data are required for useful deployment.

The script fails clearly when no compatible CUDA device exists. Hardware-specific package problems remain possible; consult the exact backend version's documentation rather than silently switching quantizers and reporting the original experiment name.

Optional private browser connection

To run the course website on the remote instance, keep it bound to loopback. From the remote project root:

bash
.venv-cloud/bin/python server.py --no-browser

From a second local PowerShell, Command Prompt, macOS, or Linux terminal:

text
ssh -p 12345 -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 root@YOUR_INSTANCE_HOST

Then open http://localhost:8765 locally. If that local port is occupied, use a different left-hand port in the forwarding command. The browser runner's new small mechanisms intentionally use the central processing unit; the optional graphics training command above runs from the remote shell.

Preserve evidence and end charges deliberately

Copy the adapter folder, reports, model-lock.json, environment file and commands back before deleting the instance. For example, from the local terminal, use the real remote path shown by pwd:

text
scp -P 12345 -r root@YOUR_INSTANCE_HOST:/ACTUAL_PROJECT_PATH/lab/outputs/nf4-train-01 ./nf4-train-01

Verify that the downloaded files open and retain model/base identity. Stopping a compute instance can leave storage allocated and billable. Destroying an instance can delete its local disk. Review the selected offer and current Vast.ai instance-management documentation; inspect the dashboard for remaining instances, volumes and charges after cleanup.

Assessment: submit local baseline measurements, the rental decision, actual hardware/package versions, a spend calculation, a verified downloaded checkpoint, reload evidence, and the cleanup record. Record failures and any unexecuted steps explicitly.

welcome:
Small Language Models From First Run to Measured Experiments

Machine Learning Super Lab • Expanded illustrated workbook • Revised November 14, 2026

This edition spells out technical abbreviations in the explanations and adds step-by-step family algorithms, worked examples and visual explanations. Literal commands and model names remain unchanged; the acronym reference explains the shortened forms inside them. Pictures are included in the accompanying compressed archive, in the images folder. The text and embedded Mermaid diagrams also describe the flows for readers using a compatible Markdown viewer.

Read in this order: mental model → machine-learning relationship → model-choice algorithm → design algorithms → learning algorithm → laboratory exercises. Use the tables and acronym reference as lookup material rather than memorizing every name before running your first model.

Start with HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, a small, dense, decoder-only Transformer. Run it on a central processing unit, understand its inputs and outputs, measure its mistakes, then train a small adapter. After that, build a tiny model from random weights and explore other architectures.

This workbook is for new machine learning engineers. You need basic computer skills; the first labs explain the Python and machine learning ideas as they appear. You do not need to rent a graphics processing unit for the core labs. The objective is to produce evidence that you understand the system: working code, repeatable experiments, honest evaluations and clear explanations.

The code is a teaching implementation. The model with 135 million parameters is deliberately modest, and the ticket dataset is deliberately small. Training a useful modern general-purpose small language model from scratch requires vastly more data and compute than these exercises. Completing the workbook develops the engineering workflow; it does not make a classroom model production-ready.

New learning paths: Pretrained versus from scratch, Deep learning workshop, Retrieval-augmented generation, and Synthetic data. The Build and retrieve track adds runnable recurrent, masked-encoder, encoder–decoder, transfer-learning, and synthetic-data experiments. The complete companion is Building-Models-and-Retrieval.md.
